abstract: The 2nd Symposium on Pharmaceutical Bioengineering and Nanobiotechnology Applied to Advanced Therapies (SBINT 2025) was held in Goiânia, Brazil, under the theme "Challenges in preclinical evaluation: paving the way to translational relevance of advanced therapies." The meeting brought together approximately 150 participants from academia, industry, clinical institutions and regulatory agencies to discuss scientific, technological and regulatory barriers shaping advanced therapy medicinal products (ATMPs) in Brazil. Keynote lectures addressed human-relevant bioengineered platforms, organ-on-a-chip and microphysiological systems, regenerative biomaterials, extracellular vesicle-based therapies, nanobiotechnology-enabled nucleic acid delivery, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-based genome and epigenome editing, and the Brazilian regulatory framework for ATMPs. The discussions highlighted the need for predictive preclinical models capable of capturing human-specific mechanisms, as conventional animal models may have limited translational value for personalized cell, gene and tissue-engineered products. Regulatory and roundtable sessions emphasized risk-based assessment, Good Manufacturing Practice-compatible infrastructure, product characterization, traceability, and the development of national biotechnological raw materials, analytical services and vector production capacity. Overall, SBINT 2025 underscored Brazil's scientific maturity and structural bottlenecks in regenerative medicine, highlighting the importance of coordinated action among academia, industry, clinical centers, regulators and funding agencies to support ATMP translation in Latin America.

title: Paving the way for translational relevance in advanced therapies in Brazil: conference report from SBINT 2025.

abstract: Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) remains difficult to cure because nucleos(t)ide analogs suppress hepatitis B virus (HBV) replication but do not eliminate covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) or integrated HBV DNA, which sustain viral RNA and hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) production. RNA-targeted therapeutics, including small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), and CRISPR-Cas13 platforms, offer sequence-directed approaches to suppress HBV transcripts and reduce antigen burden. Clinical evaluation of emerging HBV-directed therapies, including JNJ-3989, bepirovirsen, imdusiran, and related candidates, has demonstrated meaningful declines in circulating HBsAg levels. The recent phase III B-Well data further support the role of ASO-mediated antigen reduction as a potential therapeutic approach to increase the likelihood of functional cure within finite treatment regimens for selected patients. However, therapeutically induced HBsAg reduction alone rarely guarantees durable off-treatment control. This review summarizes HBV-directed RNA and oligonucleotide therapeutics from a translational pharmacology perspective, emphasizing transcript-silencing mechanisms, delivery constraints, pharmacodynamic endpoints, safety considerations, biomarker-guided patient selection, and integration with nucleos(t)ide analogs and immunomodulatory interventions. We propose that RNA-mediated antigen reduction may support finite therapy in biomarker-selected patients and may also serve as an antigen-conditioning component within staged functional cure strategies.

title: Oligonucleotide and RNA-targeted therapeutics for chronic hepatitis B: Antigen reduction, delivery, and functional cure strategies.

abstract: mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines are detectable in human blood after vaccination, but platform-specific differences in systemic persistence and transcript integrity remain poorly defined. We analyzed serial blood samples from 73 participants receiving Moderna mRNA-1273 (three formulations), Pfizer/BioNTech BNT162b2, or an investigational receptor-binding domain (RBD) mRNA vaccine (three different doses). Using droplet digital polymerase chain reaction (ddPCR) assays, we quantified total and long-range linked ("intact") vaccine mRNA, and we measured vaccine-specific ionizable lipids by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). Across platforms, mRNA decay was fastest for mRNA-1273, intermediate for BNT162b2, and slowest for the RBD vaccine, with ionizable lipid decay following the same rank order. Notably, intact spike mRNA declined 2-fold faster after mRNA-1273 than BNT162b2 vaccination. Kinetics modeling revealed platform-dependent coupling of mRNA and lipid kinetics: intact mRNA tracked closely with SM-102 for mRNA-1273, whereas ALC-0315 persisted longer than intact mRNA for BNT162b2. A ten-fragment linkage ddPCR panel spanning the spike transcript showed lower linkage toward 3'-proximal regions that mirrored the administered mRNA-1273 formulation. Together, these data provide a quantitative framework for benchmarking mRNA-LNP platform kinetics and transcript integrity in humans.

abstract: Utrophin upregulation is a promising therapeutic strategy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). Utrophin expression is post-transcriptionally repressed via microRNAs binding the 3' UTR of utrophin, particularly at the inhibitory microRNA target region (IMTR). Guide RNA pairs for editing the IMTR and a larger IMTR+ region were designed and ranked by their ability to edit and increase utrophin expression in normal and dystrophic muscle cells in vitro. Optimized guide RNA pairs and SpCas9 were used to generate MyoAAV vectors and tested for the ability to ameliorate the dystrophic phenotype of the mdx mouse model of DMD, in vivo. Systemic delivery of MyoAAV targeting the IMTR and IMTR+ using intraperitoneal injections in neonatal mdx mice resulted in efficient gene editing and increased utrophin expression in muscle. Increased utrophin was appropriately localized and accompanied by the appearance α-sarcoglycan at the sarcolemma, indicating dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex recovery. Functional analyses revealed increased specific force generation and improved resistance to eccentric contractions. Histological analyses showed a reduction in the proportion of centrally nucleated fibers that are indicative of dystrophic pathology in the mdx mice. Together, this provides proof-of-concept for a novel therapeutic strategy that, in principle, would be applicable to all patients with DMD, independent of mutation status.

abstract: Yeast platforms are rapidly transitioning from traditional eukaryotic model organisms to versatile, programmable chassis for next-generation human health applications. This review systematically examines the translational evolution of conventional and non-conventional yeasts including Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Komagataella phaffii, Saccharomyces boulardii, and Yarrowia lipolytica and redefines them as scalable biomanufacturing factories and advanced living therapeutics. We highlight milestone advancements in synthetic biology toolkits that lower technical barriers, such as CRISPR-mediated multiplex editing, modular cloning frameworks, and high-throughput secretion screening. We focus on sophisticated glycoengineering strategies for humanized N-glycosylation, alongside data-driven paradigms that leverage artificial intelligence to predict gene expression and streamline strain design. In clinical domains, we detail the established success of yeast in producing subunit or virus-like particle vaccines (e.g. HBV and HPV) and therapeutic enzymes (e.g. ecallantide), alongside its emerging role as gut-adapted live biotherapeutic products (LBPs) engineered for in situ delivery and biosensing. Finally, we explore specialized non-conventional platforms, focusing on lipid- and acetyl-CoA-rich hosts for lipophilic drug discovery, and stress-tolerant systems optimized for economical, feedstock-flexible bioprocesses. In summary, this review underscores the integrated value of yeast systems across disease modeling, industrial manufacturing, and clinical intervention, charting future directions to address global health challenges.

abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease involving abnormal keratinocyte gene expression, yet the upstream epigenetic mechanisms driving these alterations remain unclear. Here we performed multiomics analyses (chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing, CUT&Tag, ATAC-seq, and RNA sequencing) on psoriatic lesions, perilesional skin, healthy skin, and M5-stimulated HaCaT cells. Functional validation was performed using CRISPR-mediated superenhancer (SE) editing, epigenetic modulation, circular chromosome conformation capture sequencing, assay for chromatin-bound condensates by exploratory sequencing, coimmunoprecipitation, and fluorescence recovery after photobleaching. We found widespread activation of enhancers and SEs in lesions, including an interleukin 1 (IL-1)-SE regulating IL1A, IL1B, and IL36G transcription. BET inhibition reduced SE activity, repressed IL-1 cytokines, and relieved psoriasis-like inflammation in vivo. Fos-like antigen 1 (FOSL1) was identified as a key transcription factor enriched in active SEs and associated with condensate formation, contributing to the maintenance of EP300 occupancy and histone H3 lysine 27 acetylation deposition. Macrophage-derived IL-1 up-regulated FOSL1 through mitogen-activated protein kinase/ERK signaling, forming a positive feedback loop that amplified inflammation. This study revealed an FOSL1-SE-centered regulatory network driving keratinocyte inflammatory responses, providing previously unknown therapeutic targets for psoriasis.

abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Apolipoprotein C-III (apoC-III) has emerged as a validated target for lowering triglycerides, triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, and remnant cholesterol. This review summarizes the biology of apoC-III, the genetic and clinical trial evidence supporting its inhibition, and remaining questions.
RECENT FINDINGS: Loss-of-function variants in APOC3 are associated with lower levels of triglycerides and reduced cardiovascular risk. Pharmacologic inhibition of apoC-III with RNA-based agents has led to substantial reductions in apoC-III and triglycerides across familial chylomicronemia syndrome (FCS), severe hypertriglyceridemia (sHTG), and moderate hypertriglyceridemia (mHTG). In FCS, agents volanesorsen, olezarsen, and plozasiran have demonstrated reductions in triglycerides and acute pancreatitis. In sHTG, olezarsen has extended this benefit to a larger, multifactorial population. In mHTG, olezarsen and plozasiran lower triglycerides, remnant cholesterol, non-HDL-cholesterol, and apolipoprotein B, but an imaging study with olezarsen demonstrated neutral findings on coronary plaque composition, and cardiovascular event reduction has not been demonstrated. ApoC-III inhibition provides a potent strategy for lowering triglycerides and triglyceride-rich lipoproteins. Its most immediate clinical role is in FCS and sHTG, where prevention of acute pancreatitis is the main objective. Its future as a cardiovascular therapy will depend on whether reductions in remnant cholesterol and apolipoprotein B translate into fewer atherosclerotic events in a dedicated cardiovascular outcomes trial.

abstract: Efficient and cell-type-specific delivery remains a major barrier to CRISPR-based genome editing in vascular endothelial cells. Here, we systematically evaluate lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-mediated mRNA and CRISPR delivery in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs). While a conventional SM-102-based LNP formulation enables highly efficient mRNA delivery to both HEK293T cells and HUVECs, CRISPR-SpCas9 gene editing is observed exclusively in HEK293T cells, revealing strong cell-dependent limitations. We identify reduced SpCas9 mRNA translation as a key bottleneck in endothelial cells and demonstrate that rational modification of LNP lipid composition dramatically enhances SpCas9 protein expression and restores robust genome editing in HUVECs. Using the optimized LNP formulation, we achieve efficient editing of VEGFA and HIF1A in both 2D cultures and physiologically relevant 3D microfluidic endothelial systems mimicking flow conditions in vivo. Together, our results establish lipid composition as a critical determinant of endothelial CRISPR editing efficiency and provide a scalable, non-viral strategy for genome engineering in the vascular endothelium.

abstract: Gene delivery and the various routes of administration used to deliver viral vectors constitute a rapidly evolving field, with recent success in restoring hearing in children with OTOF variants in ongoing clinical otoferlin trials. With the rise of gene therapy for major hereditary hearing disorders, both syndromic and nonsyndromic, there has been parallel progress in the development of new delivery methods. Advances in intratympanic injection of antibiotics and corticosteroids, along with nearly half a century of experience in cochlear implantation surgery, have enabled multiple local and systemic approaches to access the inner ear. Recent industry investment in gene therapy and delivery technologies has accelerated scientific progress, underscoring the need for continuous evaluation of the most suitable gene delivery strategies for different causes of hearing loss. Although most gene delivery in animal models has been performed via round window membrane injection, yielding promising results in cochlear hair cell transduction, potential drawbacks remain for clinical translation-particularly limited vector distribution, which may result in a basal-to-apical gradient. Venting procedures such as stapes footplate fenestration or canalostomy have been explored to mitigate these limitations, and recent intrathecal or even in utero injections have been investigated as alternative approaches. Hearing loss can be inherited in multiple ways, and patient treatment with gene delivery, or even the type of gene therapy itself, may vary with the recent success of CRISPR/Cas-based editing tools. Understanding the genetic etiology of inner ear disorders has facilitated the identification of therapeutic targets and innovative delivery approaches. This review summarizes the current understanding of delivery routes for gene therapy, highlighting their respective strengths and limitations as demonstrated in translational and clinical research to date. Furthermore, it examines advances in drug delivery and clinical applications in the context of emerging therapeutics, providing an integrated overview and perspective on the future direction of gene delivery strategies.

abstract: Trypanosomatids are medically important single-celled eukaryotic protists with exceptional RNA biology. They display highly unusual RNA biogenesis pathways, notably mitochondrial RNA editing, an essential post-transcriptional process transforming cryptic primary transcripts into functional mRNAs. Large multiprotein assemblies coordinate the RNA editing process, in which small guide RNAs (gRNAs) anneal to the pre-mRNAs and serve as templates for uridine insertion or deletion. Kinetoplast RNA Editing Helicases (KREHs) are important components of the RNA editing process that modifies large portions of pre-mRNA via the sequential annealing and dissociation of multiple gRNAs. However, how KREH helicases interact with components of the editing machinery, and which subunits mediate these interactions, remain unresolved. Here, we examined an association between the DEAH/RHA RNA helicase KREH2 and the RESC1-RESC2 protein heterodimer using proximity labeling and co-immunoprecipitation coupled to quantitative mass spectrometry in vivo . We reconstituted a minimal trimeric KREH2 peptide-RESC1-RESC2 complex in vitro and characterized novel direct binding of a KREH2 peptide to RESC1 using cryo-electron microscopy. These results establish a mechanistic link between the RNA helicase KREH2 and the RESC1-RESC2 module at the 5'-end of gRNAs, providing new avenues for studying the orchestration of RNA remodeling in trypanosomatid mitochondrial RNA editing.

abstract: Our objective is to develop a universal gene editing therapeutic for individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF). Due to the large number of CFTR variants, we sought to develop a correction methodology utilizing targeted integration of CFTR 2-27 sequence into CFTR intron 1 (TI-1). Following electroporation of CF primary airway basal stem cells with intron 1-targeted Cas9/gRNA, we delivered CFTR 2-27 donor, flanked by a splice acceptor and polyadenylation signal, via an integrase defective lentiviral vector. Molecular characterization revealed highly efficient integration of the CFTR 2-27 sequence into the native CFTR intron 1 with most insertion events reflecting the desired homology-directed repair. Fully differentiated airway epithelium, derived from TI-1 treated basal cells without enrichment for corrected cells, exhibited functional restoration of CFTR channel activity with significant improvement of mucus hydration and transport. ATAC-seq revealed that the native CFTR chromatin architecture was unaffected by the CFTR 2-27 sequence insertion, and importantly, scRNA-seq demonstrated that the cell-type-specific expression of the introduced transgene replicated that of the endogenous CFTR. In this report, we demonstrate an almost completely mutation-agnostic therapeutic approach that is capable of functional CFTR restoration. These results may also be relevant to CFTR 2-27 integration via other editing and delivery methodologies.

abstract: Long non-coding RNAs are increasingly recognised as chromatin regulators, yet most remain functionally uncharacterised. DNAAF3-AS1, transcribed antisense to the ciliary dynein assembly factor gene DNAAF3, is almost exclusively associated with H3K36me3 in the HiMoRNA database. H3K36me3 ChIP-seq in human dermal fibroblasts following DNAAF3-AS1 knockdown with two independent antisense oligonucleotides revealed a marked reduction of gene-body H3K36me3, with residual signal shifted towards promoters. In FANTOM6 CAGE, DNAAF3-AS1 knockdown activated the p53 pathway and triggered differential promoter usage in genes enriched for p53 and apoptotic regulators. Consistently, genes that gained gene-body H3K36me3 upon knockdown were enriched for apoptosis-related pathways. In line with high expression of DNAAF3-AS1 in testis, analysis based on the adult human testis single-cell atlas suggests that DNAAF3-AS1 may contribute to promoter-level H3K36me3 regulation during late spermatogenesis. Together, these results identify DNAAF3-AS1 as a chromatin-associated lncRNA that links H3K36me3 maintenance to p53 signalling.

description:
Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality globally, with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounting for approximately 85% of all diagnoses. For patients with metastatic NSCLC lacking actionable driver mutations (e.g., EGFR, ALK), the standard first-line therapeutic strategy involves immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) targeting the programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) or programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) axis, administered either as monotherapy or in combination with platinum-doublet chemotherapy. While these regimens have significantly improved overall survival (OS), a substantial proportion of patients fail to derive durable clinical benefit, and long-term survival rates for metastatic disease remain suboptimal, often due to host-related factors that impair the anti-tumor immune response.

A critical determinant of poor therapeutic outcomes in advanced NSCLC is cancer-associated cachexia (CAC), a multifactorial paraneoplastic syndrome characterized by systemic inflammation, negative protein-energy balance, and the involuntary loss of skeletal muscle mass (sarcopenia). Primary observational studies demonstrate that nutritional derangements closely associated with cachexia - such as significant weight loss and malnutrition - are highly prevalent in lung cancer, particularly in advanced disease, with lung cancer-specific cohorts reporting rates ranging from approximately 35% - 70% depending on disease stage and assessment method. Unlike starvation, it is driven by aberrant systemic inflammation and not fully reversible via nutritional support.

Clinically, cachexia is defined by the international consensus (Fearon criteria) as weight loss \>5% over 6 months, or weight loss \>2% in individuals with a body mass index (BMI) \< 20 kg/m2 or sarcopenia. Sarcopenia is specifically defined by a low skeletal muscle index (SMI) at the L3 vertebral level, with widely validated cutoffs of \< 52.4 cm2/m2 for men and \< 8.5 cm2/m2 for women.

This is a Phase 1b/2, multi-site, single-arm, open-label, non-randomized study looking at whether adding tocilizumab to standard treatment for metastatic Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC) is safe, possible, and effective. The study includes people with metastatic NSCLC, that is lung cancer that has spread, who have experienced significant loss of weight or muscle mass.

Primary Objective Evaluate the safety/feasibility and efficacy of adding tocilizumab to standard first-line chemo-immunotherapy in biomarker-selected patients with stage IV NSCLC, defined by weight loss ≥5% within the prior 6 months, or ≥2% if BMI \< 20 kg/m².

Co-primary endpoint 1: Safety/Feasibility Proportion of patients completing four cycles of chemo-IO + tocilizumab without grade ≥3 autoimmune or non-hematological treatment-related adverse events (TRAE). Feasibility will be defined as ≥80% completion; unacceptable toxicity as \>30% incidence of grade ≥3 serious AEs.

Co-primary endpoint 2: Progression-Free Survival Rate at 6 months Proportion of patients alive and progression-free at 6 months after starting therapy per RECIST v1.1, estimated by Kaplan-Meier and presented with a 95% CI.

Secondary Objectives Assess the effect of tocilizumab on body composition, inflammatory biomarkers, and treatment response.

Secondary Endpoints: change in weight/muscle mass (CT-based sarcopenia/Fearon index); Overall Response Rate (ORR); median Overall Survival Rate; and CRP levels from baseline to end of treatment.

Correlative Objectives Evaluate associations between treatment response (PFS rate at 6 months, ORR) and baseline inflammatory biomarkers (CRP) as well as molecular biomarkers (KRAS, STK11) identified by next-generation sequencing (NGS) of tumor tissue.

Exploratory Objectives Identify associations between treatment response (PFS rate at 6 months, ORR) and longitudinal measurements of CRP, IL-6, Cyclin D1 and Bcl-xL mRNA, as well as baseline PTPRT methylation.

Participants will go through the screening and baseline process to assess eligibility. If eligible, participants will attend study treatment visits every 21 days for about 3 months, an End of Treatment (EOT) visit about 30 days after the last dose of treatment, and follow up for up to 12 months after the EOT visit. Tocilizumab will be administered in addition to standard treatment regimens for NSCLC, at a dose of 8 mg/kg intravenous (IV) once every three weeks (once every 21 days); on day one of each treatment cycle. Tocilizumab is administered as a single IV drip infusion over 1 hour; it cannot be administered as bolus or push. Tocilizumab will be given for 4 doses, at the beginning of treatment, or until disease progression or unacceptable toxicities.

The study will be open at 4 VA hospitals, and planned enrollment is about 43 participants in total with about 11 participants from each site. This research study is expected to take about 4 years. Individual participation in the study will take about 18 months.

abstract: This is a Phase 1, randomized, controlled, dose-ranging clinical trial to assess the safety and immunogenicity of novel influenza A Group 1 and influenza A Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin (HA) vaccine candidates given as intramuscular injections alone and in combination. A total of 60 healthy men and non-pregnant, non-breastfeeding women aged 18 through 59 years will be enrolled in one of 6 study arms. The 6 arms will consist of: 1) Sequential influenza A Group 1 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 (25 µg) followed by cH5/1 (25 µg), 2) Sequential influenza A Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH15/3 (25 µg) followed by cH4/3 (25 µg), 3) Sequential combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 + cH15/3 (25 µg) followed by cH5/1 + cH4/3 (25 µg), 4) A single dose of combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 + cH15/3 (50 µg) followed by placebo, 5) A single dose of combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH5/1 + cH4/3 (50 µg) followed by placebo, 6) Sequential combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 + cH15/3 (50 µg) followed by cH5/1 + cH4/3 (50 µg). The primary objectives are to evaluate safety and immunogenicity: 1) To assess the safety and reactogenicity of one or two doses of monovalent or bivalent Group 1 and 2 study products and 2) To describe the Group 1 and 2 anti-HA stalk IgG antibody responses of one or two doses of monovalent or bivalent Group 1 and 2 study products by ELISA.

abstract: Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) is a heterogeneous reproductive and endocrine disorder characterized by impaired ovarian function before the age of 40 years. Conventional management, particularly hormone therapy, addresses hypoestrogenic symptoms and long-term health risks but does not reliably restore endogenous ovarian activity or fertility. Stem cell-based strategies have therefore attracted considerable interest because of their potential paracrine, immunomodulatory, anti-apoptotic, angiogenic, and microenvironment-remodeling effects. This review summarizes current evidence on stem cell sources, therapeutic mechanisms, preclinical models, clinical studies, extracellular vesicle-based approaches, biomaterials, gene-editing strategies, and translational challenges in POI. Particular emphasis is placed on the distinction between mechanistic and animal evidence, uncontrolled or pilot human studies, and controlled clinical evidence. Across preclinical models, mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) frequently improve ovarian histology, hormone profiles, follicular parameters, and reproductive performance; however, these findings cannot be assumed to represent restoration of ovarian reserve or fertility in humans. Clinical evidence remains limited, heterogeneous, and predominantly derived from small non-randomized studies, with outcomes ranging from menstrual recovery and changes in AMH, FSH, estradiol, or antral follicle count to a small number of reported pregnancies. These surrogate changes should be distinguished from clinically meaningful endpoints such as ovulation, ongoing pregnancy, and live birth. Emerging approaches involving extracellular vesicles, biomaterials, and gene editing may improve cell retention or therapeutic potency, but most remain preclinical or early translational strategies. Overall, stem cell therapy should currently be regarded as an investigational approach for POI. Progress toward clinical translation will require standardized cell products, clearly defined dosing and administration routes, appropriate comparator groups, clinically meaningful reproductive endpoints, rigorous long-term safety surveillance, and adequately powered controlled trials.

abstract: This phase III trial tests how well the addition of dinutuximab to Induction chemotherapy along with standard of care surgical resection of the primary tumor, radiation, stem cell transplantation, and immunotherapy works for treating children with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma. Dinutuximab is a monoclonal antibody that binds to a molecule called GD2, which is found on the surface of neuroblastoma cells, but is not present on many healthy or normal cells in the body. When dinutuximab binds to the neuroblastoma cells, it helps signal the immune system to kill the tumor cells. This helps the cells of the immune system kill the cancer cells, this is a type of immunotherapy. When chemotherapy and immunotherapy are given together, during the same treatment cycle, it is called chemoimmunotherapy. This clinical trial randomly assigns patients to receive either standard chemotherapy and surgery or chemoimmunotherapy (chemotherapy plus dinutuximab) and surgery during Induction therapy. Chemotherapy drugs administered during Induction include, cyclophosphamide, topotecan, cisplatin, etoposide, vincristine, and doxorubicin. These drugs work in different ways to stop the growth of cancer cells, either by killing the cells, by stopping them from dividing or by stopping them from spreading. Upon completion of 5 cycles of Induction therapy, a disease evaluation is completed to determine how well the treatment worked. If the tumor responds to therapy, patients receive a tandem transplantation with stem cell rescue. If the tumor has little improvement or worsens, patients receive chemoimmunotherapy on Extended Induction. During Extended Induction, dinutuximab is given with irinotecan, temozolomide. Patients with a good response to therapy move on to Consolidation therapy, when very high doses of chemotherapy are given at two separate points to kill any remaining cancer cells. Following, transplant, radiation therapy is given to the site where the cancer originated (primary site) and to any other areas that are still active at the end of Induction. The final stage of therapy is Post-Consolidation. During Post-Consolidation, dinutuximab is given with isotretinoin, with the goal of maintaining the response achieved with the previous therapy. Adding dinutuximab to Induction chemotherapy along with standard of care surgical resection of the primary tumor, radiation, stem cell transplantation, and immunotherapy may be better at treating children with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma.
description:
PRIMARY OBJECTIVE:

I. To determine if the event-free survival (EFS) of patients with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma assigned to early chemoimmunotherapy during Induction differs from that of patients who are not assigned to treatment that includes early chemoimmunotherapy.

SECONDARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To determine if early chemoimmunotherapy during Induction therapy improves end of Induction (EOI) response rates and overall survival (OS) for patients with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma.

II. To determine response rates, EFS, and OS following an Extended Induction regimen with chemoimmunotherapy in patients with progressive disease or a poor response to Induction therapy.

III. To compare the toxicities experienced by patients treated with chemoimmunotherapy during Induction versus those experienced by patients treated with standard Induction and to describe toxicities experienced during Extended Induction.

IV. To determine GD2 expression on tumor tissue and tumor cells in bone marrow and assess for associations with response and outcome.

EXPLORATORY OBJECTIVES:

I. To describe the association between tumor and host factors and outcomes in patients receiving protocol therapy.

II. To evaluate circulating biomarkers and markers of minimal residual disease at baseline and during therapy, and assess for associations with response and outcome.

III. To compare patterns of failure between patients treated with and without dinutuximab during induction.

IV. To determine the effect of telomere maintenance mechanisms on end of Induction response rates, EFS, and OS.

V. To explore the impact of high-risk neuroblastoma (HRNBL) and its therapy, including the addition of dinutuximab to Induction chemotherapy, on functional and quality of life outcomes in patients with HRNBL, as measured by caregiver (parent/legal guardian) and patient questionnaires.

VI. To describe the adequacy of diagnostic biopsy specimens, including those obtained by percutaneous core needle biopsy.

VII. To explore the associations between family-reported adverse social determinants of health and both clinical outcomes and biology.

VIII. To develop and validate deep learning predictors of Induction response based on diagnostic MIBG scans. (Imaging Objective) IX. To compare institutional versus central determination of overall response, individual response components (primary tumor, soft tissue and bone metastatic disease, and bone marrow metastatic disease), and poor end of induction response (PEIR) and good end of induction response (GEIR) determination. (Imaging Objective) X. To describe late toxicities (including impaired organ function, neuropsychiatric toxicity, and incidence of secondary malignancy) in patients treated with dinutuximab during Induction or Extended Induction to late toxicities in patients who have not received dinutuximab during these phases of therapy.

XI. To evaluate whether reduced dose radiotherapy to the primary site clinical target volume (CTV) in patients with complete response of the primary site at EOI results in comparable local control relative to historical cohorts.

XII. To compare post-transplant complications between treatment arms, and assess for associations with outcome.

XIII. To assess for associations between EOI response (including good end of Induction response \[GEIR\] and poor end of Induction response \[PEIR\]) and individual response components (primary tumor, soft tissue and bone metastatic disease, and bone marrow metastatic disease) with outcome (EFS and OS).

XIV. To describe and compare the changes in image-defined risk factors (IDRFs) between patients treated with and without dinutuximab during Induction and associate with surgical outcomes and local failure rates following primary tumor resection.

XV. To bank serial samples of blood, bone marrow, and tumor tissue for future research.

OUTLINE: Patients receive Induction cycle 1 and are then randomized to 1 of 2 treatment arms.

INDUCTION CYCLE 1: Patients receive cyclophosphamide intravenously (IV) over 30 minutes and topotecan IV over 30 minutes on days 1-5 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity.

ARM A:

INDUCTION CYCLES 2-5: Patients receive cyclophosphamide IV over 30 minutes and topotecan IV over 30 minutes on days 1-5 of cycle 2 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients then undergo stem cell harvest via apheresis. Patients then receive cisplatin IV over 4 hours and etoposide IV over 2 hours on days 1-3 of cycles 3 and 5, and vincristine IV on day 1, doxorubicin IV over 15 minutes, and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days 1-2 of cycle 4 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients undergo primary tumor resection after Induction cycle 4 or 5. Following Induction cycle 5, patients undergo testing to determine response to Induction therapy. Patients with a good tumor response proceed to Consolidation, while patients with a poor tumor response proceed to Extended Induction.

EXTENDED INDUCTION: Patients with a poor tumor response or progression during Induction receive temozolomide orally (PO), via nasogastric tube (NG), or via gastric tube (G-tube) on days 1-5, irinotecan IV over 90 minutes on days 1-5, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours. Treatment repeats every 21 days for up to a maximum of 6 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. If at any time during Extended Induction testing shows a good tumor response, patients proceed to Consolidation. If after 6 cycles of Extended Induction or if at any time progression is noted, patients are removed from the study.

CONSOLIDATION: Patients undergo two autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantations (HSCTs) during Consolidation. Patients receive thiotepa IV over 2 hours on days -7 to -5 and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days -5 to -2 during HSCT 1. Patients then receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between 6 and 10 weeks after stem cell infusion, patients receive melphalan IV over 30 minutes on days -7 to -5, etoposide IV over 24 hours on days -7 to -4, and carboplatin over 24 hours on days -7 to -4 during HSCT 2. Patients receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between day +42 and day +80 after HSCT 2. Patients receive radiation daily for 12 treatments in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity.

POST CONSOLIDATION: Patients receive dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 4-7 and isotretinoin PO twice daily (BID) on days 11-24 of cycles 1-5. Treatment repeats every 28 days for up to 5 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. Patients then receive isotretinoin PO BID on days 15-28 for 1 additional cycle, cycle 6.

Patients undergo blood and urine sample collection, echocardiogram (ECHO) or multigated acquisition scan (MUGA), bone marrow aspiration and/or biopsy, computed tomography (CT) scan, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), iodine-123 meta-iodobenzylguanidine (I-MIBG) scan and possible fluorodeoxyglucose position emission tomography (FDG-PET) scan throughout the study.

ARM B:

INDUCTION CYCLES 2-5: Patients receive cyclophosphamide IV over 30 minutes, topotecan IV over 30 minutes on days 1-5, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 2-5 of cycle 2 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients then undergo stem cell harvest via apheresis. Patients receive cisplatin IV over 4 hours and etoposide IV over 2 hours on days 1-3 and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 2-5 of cycles 3 and 5, and vincristine IV on day 1, doxorubicin IV over 15 minutes, and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days 1-2, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 2-5 of cycle 4 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients undergo primary tumor resection after Induction cycle 4 or 5. Following Induction cycle 5, patients undergo testing to determine response to Induction therapy. Patients with a good tumor response proceed to Consolidation, while patients with a poor tumor response proceed to Extended Induction.

EXTENDED INDUCTION: Patients with a poor tumor response or progression during Induction receive temozolomide PO, via NG tube, or via G-tube on days 1-5, irinotecan IV over 90 minutes on days 1-5, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours. Treatment repeats every 21 days for up to a maximum of 6 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. If at any time during Extended Induction testing shows a good tumor response, patients proceed to Consolidation. If after 6 cycles of Extended Induction or if at any time progression is noted, patients are removed from the study.

CONSOLIDATION: Patients undergo two autologous HSCTs during Consolidation. Patients receive thiotepa IV over 2 hours on days -7 to -5 and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days -5 to -2 during HSCT 1. Patients then receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between 6 and 10 weeks after stem cell infusion patients receive melphalan IV over 30 minutes on days -7 to -5, etoposide IV over 24 hours on days -7 to -4, and carboplatin over 24 hours on days -7 to -4 during HSCT 2. Patients receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between day +42 and day +80 after HSCT 2, patients receive radiation daily for 12 treatments in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity.

POST CONSOLIDATION: Patients receive dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 4-7 and isotretinoin PO BID on days 11-24 of cycles 1-5. Treatment repeats every 28 days for up to 5 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. Patients then receive isotretinoin PO BID on days 15-28 for 1 additional cycle, cycle 6.

Patients undergo blood and urine sample collection, ECHO or MUGA, bone marrow aspiration and/or biopsy, CT scan, MRI, I-MIBG scan and possible FDG-PET scan throughout the study.

After completion of study treatment, patients are followed up at 3, 6, 9,12, 15, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 54, and 60 months and then periodically for up to 10 years from enrollment.

outcomes.description: EFS time is calculated from time of randomization to Arms A or B to first episode of disease relapse or progression, second malignancy, or death, or until last contact if no event has occurred.
outcomes.measure: Event free survival (EFS)

outcomes.description: The response rate will be calculated among all evaluable patients at end of Induction. Responders are defined as patients who achieve a \>= partial response per the revised 2017 International Neuroblastoma Response Criteria (INRC)
outcomes.measure: End of Induction (EOI) response rate
outcomes.time_frame: From randomization to end of extended Induction, up to 12 months

outcomes.description: OS time is calculated from time of randomization to Arms A or B until death, or until last contact if patient is alive.
outcomes.measure: Overall survival (OS)

outcomes.description: The proportion of patients with at least one grade 3 or higher non-hematologic toxicity or grade 4 or higher hematologic toxicity during protocol therapy, graded according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0, will be reported.
outcomes.measure: Incidence of adverse events

outcomes.description: Dinutuximab binding to pre-therapy patient tumor samples will be measured and categorized as high or low.
outcomes.measure: GD2 expression

outcomes.description: A series of univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards (for EFS and OS) and logistic regression (for responders vs. non-responders) models will be fit for patients in Arms A and B to evaluate the relationship between tumor and host factors (including tumor ALK and other somatic mutations, copy-number aberrations, gene fusions, gene expression, and pathogenic germline variants) and chemo-immunotherapy during Induction with outcome.
outcomes.measure: Association between tumor and host factors and outcomes

outcomes.description: Will be assessed by comparing the proportion of patients with detectable vs. non-detectable tumor markers (including circulating tumor deoxyribonucleic acid, circulating free DNA, circulating tumor cells, and immune function profiling) between Arms A and B during and after induction and post-consolidation therapy using chi-squared tests at each individual time point, and Cochran's Q across time points to determine if there is a consistent difference in proportions between arms across time. In addition, the tumor markers will be analyzed as continuous variables using longitudinal data analysis methodology such as mixed effects models or generalized estimating equations as appropriate.
outcomes.measure: Circulating biomarkers and markers of minimal residual disease

outcomes.description: The impact of early or late chemoimmunotherapy during Induction on the probability of the involvement of a specific disease site at first relapse will be evaluated using Fisher's exact test.
outcomes.measure: Patterns of failure

outcomes.description: A series of univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards (for EFS and OS) and logistic regression (for responders vs. non-responders) models will be fit for patients in arms A and B to evaluate the relationship between telomere maintenance mechanism and chemoimmunotherapy during Induction with outcome. Patients will be classified into 3 groups by telomere maintenance mechanism (TMM) based on messenger ribonucleic acid expression of TERT and analysis of telomeric DNA C-circles: telomerase (TERT) positive, alternative of lengthening of telomeres (ALT) positive, or no identified TMM.
outcomes.measure: Effect of telomere maintenance mechanisms

abstract: Systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX)-based aptamer discovery can be constrained by target availability, selection biases, and optimization requirements. We introduce Xelari, a modular pipeline for de novo DNA and RNA aptamer design from protein structures without target-specific SELEX data or retraining. Xelari combines algorithmic modules with surrogate models trained on physical or structural references. InNA reproduced nucleotide-amino-acid interaction energies with RMSE of 0.19 kcal/mol across 483,735 reference pairs. AliNA achieved a mean F1 of 0.757 on 339 PDB-derived RNA evaluation sequences. Edgar correlated with experimental folding energies but did not reproduce their absolute scale, supporting its use as a ranking heuristic. Under the reported calibration, ValentiNA showed MAE of 0.931 kcal/mol and Spearman ρ of 0.795 across 32 retrospective records associated with 27 structural templates; this analysis does not establish family-independent validation. Prospectively, three DNA aptamers designed against Treponema pallidum protein structures showed cell-associated binding in a treponeme assay (apparent KD, 0.91-2.57 μM). A fourth DNA aptamer served as a capture reagent in a serum-based hybrid aptamer-antibody assay for Tau441. These applications support feasibility without establishing intended-target engagement in the cellular assay or a general success rate, positioning structure-based design as a complement to experimental selection.

abstract: Sugar crops including sugarcane, sugar beets, and sweet sorghum, are fundamental for global sucrose supply and crucial feedstocks for bioethanol production and industrial bioproducts. However, yield and sucrose accumulation are significantly influenced by abiotic stresses, including drought, salinity/alkalinity, heat, chilling/freezing, and heavy metal toxicity. The polygenic complexity of stress tolerance, particularly in sugarcane with its large, polyploid, and haplotype-diverse genome, presents significant challenges for conventional breeding, rendering it slow and imprecise. This review combines advances in genome-editing technologies, including CRISPR/Cas systems (Cas9 and Cas12a), along with transcriptional techniques (CRISPRa/i), base editors, and prime editors. These tools, combined with the progress in reference genomes, haplotype-resolved assemblies, and pangenomes, have facilitated precise gene discovery, genomic selection, and targeted editing. CRISPR-based approaches offer promising avenues for enhancing key stress-responsive pathways governing oxidative homeostasis, membrane integrity, osmotic regulation, hormone signaling, and ion-homeostasis in sugar crops. Prominent candidate targets include transcription factors (TF), signaling components, raffinose biosynthesis genes implicated in freezing tolerance, regulators of salt and alkaline stress, and determinants of heavy metal tolerance and sequestration. Translational challenges, such as off-target effects, low transformation efficiencies, and editing multiple homologues or haplotypes, are being addressed such as DNA-free ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery, high-throughput screening, haplotype-specific target design, and haplotype-aware guide RNA engineering based on unique genetic variation sites across different gene haplotypes. Collectively, the integration of advanced CRISPR toolkits with enhanced genomic information resources and phenotyping capabilities holds significant potential for accelerating the development of precision-bred, multi-stress-resilient sugar crops that sustain yield, quality, and industrial value under abiotic stress conditions.

abstract: A central strategy in treating neurodegenerative disorders, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), is lowering levels of disease-driving proteins. Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) offer a direct RNA-targeted approach to reduce protein expression, but experimental discovery and optimization are constrained by small, heterogeneous datasets and target-specific variability. Computational models that predict ASO knockdown efficacy directly from sequence and context could improve candidate selection, yet generalization across gene families and experimental settings remains challenging. In this study, we present a biophysics-based computational framework for predicting RNase H-active ASO knockdown efficacy under small-data constraints. We curate and integrate heterogeneous literature-derived ASO efficacy measurements into a unified dataset and evaluate model transfer using independently generated experimental ASOs targeting ALS-relevant genes DAZAP1 and FAM69C. Knockdown efficacy is defined at the transcript level (%KD), providing a mechanistic measure of RNase H-mediated activity. To our knowledge, this is the first framework that combines ASO feature engineering with one-shot family calibration for prediction under realistic small-data conditions. We integrate sequence representations with physics-based features capturing RNA-DNA hybridization thermodynamics, targeting RNA accessibility. Compared to sequence-only baselines, this mechanistic feature augmentation reduces external wet-lab prediction error, improving generalization to independent experimental data. Despite these gains, uncalibrated predictions exhibit systematic target-family-specific scale bias. We address this challenge by using a minimal one-shot family calibration strategy that applies an additive offset derived from a single experimentally measured reference ASO per new target family. We further assess the model's behavior using a leave-one-family-out simulation on literature-derived ASO families, repeatedly applying one-shot calibration to quantify its expected benefit and variability under controlled small-n conditions. One-shot calibration markedly improves absolute prediction accuracy while preserving within-family ranking, without retraining or increasing model complexity. Out-of-distribution evaluation shows stable performance for DAZAP1 and increased uncertainty for FAM69C, consistent with the expected effects of very small sample sizes. Permutation-based interpretability analyses show that predictive signal is dominated by global sequence architecture, with thermodynamic and accessibility features providing correlated, secondary contributions. Together, these results establish a computational workflow in which literature-trained models can be transferred to new target genes using minimal experimental input, supporting systematic ASO prioritization in small-data models.

abstract: PRE-EMPT will assemble a cohort of 150 participants from three populations (low risk, intermediate risk, and high risk for self-harm). We will obtain clinical assessments, structural and functional MRI utilizing tasks pioneered by our team to assess cognitive control (CC) and emotion regulation (ER), and peripheral circular RNA (circRNA) levels to characterize the molecular brain states associated with behavioral risk. The clinical, imaging, and transcriptomic data will be fused and jointly analyzed to increase the accuracy of our risk prediction models. PRE-EMPT in three separate Aims will then prospectively assess three promising and innovative interventions for their potential to reduce suicidal ideation and alter activity in key neural networks: 1) neurofeedback (NF) using real-time fMRI with simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG), 2) a form of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) called accelerated intermittent theta burst stimulation (aiTBS) with dose optimization through electric field modeling; and 3) psilocybin assisted therapy (PSI), with flexible dosing plan to maximize the depth of psychedelic experience. These therapies were chosen based on our team's prior work in all three interventions demonstrating rapid action and large effects.

description:
This is a first in human Phase I study of RNA-LP vaccines for newly diagnosed adult MGMT unmethylated (low level or undetected) glioblastoma (GBM) and pediatric patients with newly diagnosed HGG (pHGG). The phase I portion of the study will involve a dose-escalation study to identify the maximally tolerated dose (MTD). The GBM portion of the study is single site (UF) and the pediatric portion will be multisite.

This clinical trial will consist of three parts: Surgery, Radiation, and Immunotherapy. Surgery and chemoradiation will be standard of care for patients with GBM. Potentially eligible participants will be enrolled on a screening consent for the sterile collection of tumor material in a manner suitable for RNA extraction, amplification, and loading of lipid particles (LPs). Pediatric participants will have tumor material sent to the University of Florida (UF) from qualified PNOC sites. Adult GBM participants must have surgery for collection of tumor material at the University of Florida. Following surgical resection with confirmatory pathologic diagnosis, patients will be enrolled in the trial after informed consent has been obtained.

The RNA-LP vaccination will begin within 4 weeks following radiation and after review of post-radiation MRI (for baseline). After radiation patients will receive three RNA-LP vaccines every 2 weeks before beginning 12 cycles of adjuvant monthly RNA- LP vaccines for a total of 15 vaccines.

Participants may receive RNA-LP vaccines for up to 14 months.

Participants will be followed until death due to any cause. MRI and clinical evaluation for assessment of disease progression will be conducted every 3 months for the first-year post-immunotherapy and then every 6-12 months over the next 2 years.

outcomes.description:
A DLT will be defined as any immunotherapy-related (possible, probable or definite):

* Grade ≥ 3 non-hematologic toxicity that does not improve to ≤ Grade 2 within 72 hours; hepatic or renal dysfunction that does not improve to ≤ grade 2 within 7 days
* Grade ≥3 cytokine release syndrome that does not improve to ≤ Grade 2 within 72 hours
* Grade ≥ 3 encephalopathy as defined by the American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy (ASTCT) Consensus Immune Effector Cell-Associated Encephalopathy criteriaGrade 3 or greater non-neurologic, non-hematologic toxicity
* Grade 3 neurologic toxicity that does not improve to Grade II or better within 7 days
* Grade 3-4 hematologic toxicity that does not improve to Grade 2 or better within 14 days
* Grade 3 autoimmune encephalomyelitis
* Grade 4 neurologic toxicity.
outcomes.measure: Safety of RNA-LP vaccine

outcomes.description: The Phase I Stratum 1 dose-escalation study will be performed in up to 28 adult participants using a Bayesian optimal interval (BOIN) design with an initial embedded accelerated titration design (ATD) to efficiently identify the maximally tolerated dose (MTD). For the initial ATD, patients will be enrolled and treated in cohorts of size 1 starting at dose level -4 to dose level -1. After the first DLT is observed or if dose level 0 is reached without prior DLT in dose level -4 to -1, the study will expand to a BOIN design with a cohort size of 3 to identify the MTD. For the initial ATD, patients will be enrolled and treated in cohorts of size 1 starting at dose level -4 to dose level -1, and will expand to a cohort size of 3 after the first DLT is observed or at dose level 0. There are 8 dose levels to potentially be assessed including the possibility of 4 dose levels for the ATD and 4 for the BOIN.
outcomes.measure: Determination of Maximum Tolerated Dose

abstract: Curative therapies for genetic diseases caused by pathogenic mutations demand precise and safe genome editing technologies. Prime editing (PE), a CRISPR-Cas9-derived technology that enables precise base conversions without double-strand breaks (DSBs), has emerged as a transformative tool with the ability to correct 89% of human pathogenic mutations. However, transitioning PE from preclinical models to clinical applications faces critical challenges, particularly in the development of in vivo delivery systems and scalable manufacturing. This review systematically summarizes advances of in vivo PE therapeutics, focusing on the therapeutic outcomes across some retinal, metabolic, and hematologic genetic diseases. We further dissect barriers to clinical translation, including in the immunogenicity of viral vectors, off-target risks in nondividing cells, and large-scale production bottlenecks. By highlighting the unique advantages of in vivo PE and proposing actionable solutions for scalable manufacturing, the work provides a roadmap for accelerating in vivo PE-based therapies toward clinical reality.

title: Research progress of gene correction for genetic diseases via in vivo prime editing.

abstract: Cisplatin-based chemotherapy constitutes the cornerstone of first-line treatment for muscle-invasive and metastatic bladder cancer (BCa); however, the frequent emergence of chemoresistance presents a formidable clinical obstacle. In the present study, by combining a systematic CRISPR-Cas9 E3 ligase library screen with drug sensitivity data from the GDSC database, DCST1 (DC-STAMP Domain Containing 1) was identified as a pivotal driver of cisplatin resistance. DCST1 expression was found to be markedly upregulated in chemoresistant BCa tissues, and its elevated expression served as an independent predictor of poor patient prognosis. Functionally, DCST1 deficiency sensitizes BCa cells to cisplatin in vitro and in vivo by triggering PANoptosis (simultaneous apoptosis, pyroptosis, and necroptosis). Mechanistically, DCST1 functions as an atypical E3 ubiquitin ligase to catalyze the K11/K27-linked polyubiquitination of NFAT5 at residue K450. This non-canonical ubiquitination stabilizes NFAT5 by preventing its lysosomal degradation and promotes its nuclear accumulation. Nuclear NFAT5 then transcriptionally activates SOD2, orchestrating an anti-PANoptotic program that ensures BCa cell survival under chemotherapeutic stress. Furthermore, through molecular docking and CETSA validation, digoxin was identified as a potent pharmacological inhibitor of NFAT5 that overcomes DCST1-mediated chemoresistance and synergistically restores cisplatin sensitivity. Collectively, these findings unveil a previously unrecognized ubiquitination-dependent mechanism of chemoresistance and establish the DCST1-NFAT5 signaling axis as a promising therapeutic target for overcoming drug resistance in BCa.

title: DCST1 drives cisplatin resistance via non-canonical ubiquitination and stabilization of NFAT5 to suppress PANoptosis in bladder cancer.

abstract: Kabuki syndrome type 1 (KS1) is a rare cause of intellectual disability resulting from heterozygous pathogenic variants in the gene encoding the histone methyltransferase KMT2D. A previously established loss-of-function mouse model of KS1 exhibits key phenotypic features, and therapeutic trials in this mouse model suggest postnatal malleability of neurological symptoms. However, 15-30% of individuals with KS1 carry missense variants. To investigate whether missense variants lead to similar phenotypic presentation in mice, we used CRISPR-Cas9 to introduce the KS1 patient variant R5179H, corresponding to R5230H in mice, into C57BL/6NTac animals. Computational and in vitro testing suggested that the R5230H variant does not impair protein stability or enzyme function of KMT2D. Despite a distinct mechanistic basis, our new mouse model (Kmt2d+/R5230H) recapitulated most phenotypes of our prior loss-of-function model, including growth deficiency, craniofacial anomalies and IgA deficiency, but not altered neurological function. Kmt2d+/R5230H mice showed perinatal lethality and a high frequency of unilateral kidney agenesis, a novel phenotype in KS1 mouse models. Kmt2d+/R5230H mice provide a unique opportunity to understand the impact of missense variants on KMT2D function and uncover developmental and perinatal abnormalities in KS1.

title: A patient-derived missense mouse model of Kabuki syndrome 1.

abstract: CD8+ T cells directly target and kill cancer cells and are required for effective antitumor immunity. However, CD8+ T cells may become dysfunctional when exposed to chronic antigen stimulation during cancer. Dysfunction is characterized by reduced proliferation, increased expression of inhibitory receptors, and impaired effector function, yet the genetic mechanisms controlling dysfunction remain poorly understood. Therefore, we developed a murine ex vivo chronic stimulation model that recapitulates features of CD8+ T cell dysfunction observed within the tumor microenvironment. By coupling this system with genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 loss-of-function screening, we discovered that the progression of murine CD8+ T cells to a dysfunctional state required eIF4G2, a noncanonical mRNA translation factor. Deletion of eIF4G2 restored CD8+ T cell survival and proliferation during chronic stimulation conditions in vitro. Transcriptomic, proteomic, and flow cytometric analyses revealed that eIF4G2 deletion shifts CD8+ T cell phenotype from a dysfunctional state to a proliferative state. eIF4G2 depletion reduced oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and accumulation of misfolded protein aggresomes during chronic in vitro stimulation. Finally, eIF4G2-depleted cells mediated enhanced tumor control in a murine model of melanoma. These data suggest that targeting eIF4G2 may promote CD8+ T cell resilience and improve therapeutic antitumor immunity.

title: CRISPR-Cas9 screen identifies eIF4G2 as a regulator of CD8+ T cell dysfunction.

abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and deadly primary brain tumor in adults, characterized by diffuse infiltrative lesions, distinct oncogenic alterations, and a suppressive tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). These traits, however, are not fully recapitulated in current syngeneic murine glioma models, thereby limiting the pre-clinical development of novel therapies. Here we developed murine GBM models with patient-specific mutations that shared striking resemblance with human disease. Mosaic analysis with dual-recombinase mediated cassette exchange (MADR) and CRISPR-Cas9 were leveraged to generate autochthonous tumor models with single-copy somatic transgenesis of murine epidermal growth factor receptor variant III (mEGFRvIII) and loss-of-function mutations commonly observed in GBM. Characterization of a model lacking Pten and Cdkn2a (mEGFRvIII-PC) via histopathologic analyses, functional assays, and single-cell RNA sequencing showed these tumors developed as diffuse, infiltrative lesions with ill-defined margins and a necrotic core. The TIME was primarily comprised of microglia with minimal lymphocyte infiltration, recapitulating patient tumors. Furthermore, these tumors displayed intrinsic resistance to immune checkpoint blockade, potentially due to poor myeloid cell antigen presentation and T cell priming. Additionally, mEGFRvIII-PC cells were the most resistant to antigen-specific T cell-induced cytotoxicity and simultaneously promoted T cell exhaustion, while murine interferon-γ (mIFN-γ) stimulation induced a greater response in vitro with enhanced upregulation of PD-L1 relative to MHC-I. In sum, these findings demonstrate the improved fidelity of the mEGFRvIII-PC model to patient tumors and support its use in developing and refining novel therapeutic paradigms for GBM.

title: A syngeneic murine glioma model recapitulates key molecular, immunologic, and functional features of human glioblastoma to enable therapeutic development.

abstract: Simultaneous detection of dual microRNA biomarkers is crucial for accurate prognosis and treatment monitoring of cervical spondylosis, yet remains challenging due to the lack of stringent logic control and high-fidelity signal amplification. Herein, we report an AND-gate-controlled colorimetric assay that integrates target-recycling strand displacement amplification, CRISPR/Cas13a/crRNA-mediated trans-cleavage, and self-priming cyclic amplification for sensitive and specific analysis of two cervical spondylosis-associated miRNAs (miRNA-221 and miRNA-146a). Only when both targets are present does the cascade proceed, producing double-stranded amplicons that trigger SYBR Green I-catalyzed TMB oxidation, yielding a naked-eye-visible blue signal. The assay exhibits a broad linear range from 10 fM to 500 pM, a detection limit of 2.12 fM, excellent selectivity, and good repeatability. Importantly, we applied this method to clinically evaluate the therapeutic effect of auricular point pressing (ear acupressure), a traditional Chinese medicine intervention for cervical spondylosis. In a 4-week study of 20 patients, the treatment group receiving auricular point pressing showed significant downregulation of both miRNAs compared to baseline, while the control group showed no notable change. Results correlated well with RT-qPCR, confirming reliability. This logic-controlled CRISPR/Cas13a platform offers a robust, equipment-free strategy for early prognosis of cervical spondylosis and objective monitoring of auricular point pressing therapy.

title: AND-gate CRISPR/Cas13a-assisted colorimetric assay for dual microRNA monitoring of cervical spondylosis prognosis and auricular point pressing therapy evaluation.

abstract: Hearing loss is a prevalent sensory disorder with profound social and health impacts. Although hearing aids and cochlear implants can significantly restore auditory perception, they do not address the underlying genetic causes. Inherited forms of hearing loss, often monogenic, are ideal candidates for gene therapy, particularly since over 150 genes have been linked to deafness. Advances in vector engineering and genome editing technologies now enable precise targeting of auditory cells within the inner ear. Technologies such as Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats-Cas systems, base editing, and prime editing offer powerful tools to correct pathogenic variants at their native genomic loci. This review summarizes the current landscape of gene editing approaches for both hereditary and acquired hearing loss, emphasizing key preclinical studies in mouse models encompassing dominant and recessive forms of deafness. We discuss the advantages and limitations of different editing techniques, vector delivery systems, and administration routes, and explore obstacles including editing efficiency, cell-specific targeting, and the translation of these therapies to humans. Collectively, these advances represent a pivotal step toward variant-specific, durable, and potentially curative treatments for hearing loss.

title: Emerging Therapies for Genetic Deafness: The Rise of Precision Gene Editing.

abstract: Experimental oncofertility remains fragmented across models of cancer biology, treatment-associated gonadotoxicity, fertility preservation, and reproductive recovery. We propose extending the Oncopig concept into a translational platform that reconnects these states within one genetically defined, cancer-bearing host. The Oncopig provides the oncologic backbone, combining programmable cancer in an immunocompetent large-animal host with clinically scaled intervention and longitudinal sampling. High-resolution porcine genomics, CRISPR-based genome engineering, somatic-cell nuclear transfer for line generation, comparative experimental pathology, and mature reproductive biotechnology extend this architecture toward reproductive endpoints. Here, programmability refers to deliberate specification of the cancer state-genotype, cell lineage or induction strategy, and timing-whereas the reproductive phenotype is measured longitudinally rather than programmed. Distant-cancer modules can test whether cancer status modifies gonadotoxicity, while reproductive-organ modules require disease-specific alleles, appropriate cell-of-origin targeting, and pathology-led validation. Because porcine and human reproduction align in several endocrine and gonadal processes but differ in cycle organization, implantation, placentation, and pregnancy, translation should emphasize process-level endpoints rather than numerical equivalence. The platform is particularly suited to unresolved questions involving targeted therapies and immunotherapies, preservation timing, and pediatric or prepubertal patients. Porcine reproductive biotechnology provides functional endpoints from gonadal tissue and gametes to embryos and offspring. Rather than replacing rodent or human-based models, the Oncopig framework adds an integrated translational layer for questions requiring clinically scaled intervention, longitudinal physiology, and functional reproductive recovery.

title: The minipig as a programmable translational platform for experimental oncofertility.

abstract: Pyroptosis is a form of programmed cell death characterized by activation of inflammasome complexes and caspase signaling cascades, ultimately leading to the cleavage and activation of pore‑forming executioners such as gasdermin D (GSDMD), ‑E and ‑B. Accumulating evidence indicates that pyroptosis induction in cancer cells exerts potent antitumor effects. As a result, recent therapeutic strategies such as cancer nanotherapy have increasingly focused on harnessing pyroptotic cell death to improve cancer treatment outcomes. This review aimed to explore recent advances in nanotechnology‑based approaches designed to induce pyroptosis in cancer cells, with an emphasis on their potential to enhance antitumor immunity and overcome treatment resistance. It explored four distinct nanoplatforms: i) Chemo‑photodynamic systems that trigger GSDME‑mediated death by generating reactive oxygen species; ii) magneto‑plasmonic nanoparticles that use GSDME activation to modulate the tumor microenvironment, turning 'cold' tumors 'hot'; iii) bioorthogonal chemical delivery tools leveraging click chemistry for site‑specific gasdermin release; and iv) nano‑CRISPR activation scaffolds designed to boost GSDME expression and work alongside cisplatin. Beyond these platforms, the present review highlights how immune cell‑derived granzymes and interferon‑γ drive vital downstream pyroptotic pathways via GSDME and GSDMB activation. Lastly, the review weighs clinical risks, such as chronic systemic inflammation and tumor‑promoting environments, providing a realistic perspective on how to safely progress these preclinical nanotherapies into selective, effective clinical immunotherapies.

title: Pyroptosis in cancer nanotherapy: Molecular mechanisms and advanced nanosystems (Review).

abstract: Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy is a heritable cardiac disorder commonly linked to alterations in desmosomal proteins. While desmosomal dysfunction is a recognized pathogenic mechanism, the early molecular remodeling that precedes clinical manifestations remains unclear. Here we used a mouse model with inducible cardiomyocyte-specific knockout of Pkp2 (encoding plakophilin-2) and performed time-resolved mass spectrometry-based proteomics to map disease progression from early PKP2 loss to structural remodeling. Molecular changes preceded phenotypic abnormalities, and spatial asymmetry was evident, with earlier and more pronounced proteome remodeling in the right ventricle despite comparable PKP2 depletion in both ventricles. Downregulation of protein networks spanning desmosomes, sarcomeres and mitochondria suggests their functional coupling, with mitochondrial remodeling emerging as an early and progressively worsening feature. Intervention with honokiol attenuated changes across the major protein networks, highlighting mitochondrial pathways as promising therapeutic targets and honokiol as a potential strategy to delay arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy progression. Our findings provide critical insights into the concealed stage of disease progression and identify molecular targets for early intervention.

title: Temporal proteomics maps concealed-stage remodeling and reveals early mitochondrial alteration as an intervention target in a model of PKP2-arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) and autophagy-lysosome pathway constitute the core proteolytic metabolic networks that maintain cellular protein homeostasis (proteostasis) and organelle metabolic identity. Intracellular pathogens frequently reprogram host metabolic pathways to establish replicative niches, yet how they manipulate proteostatic metabolism to remodel organelle maturation remains incompletely understood.
METHODS: CelF secretion was confirmed by TEM translocation assay. CRISPR-dCas9 was used to generate CelF knockdown and complementation strains, with celF transcription verified by RT-qPCR. Cell infection and SCID mouse models were used to assess intracellular survival, Coxiella-containing vacuole (CCV) maturation, and virulence of Coxiella burnetii. The effect of CelF on late autophagy was examined by dual-fluorescence LC3 and Western blotting. Then, UBQLN1 was identified as a CelF-interacting host protein by co-IP and pull-down, followed by truncation mapping. Finally, co-IP, UBQLN1 knockdown, Western blotting and MST assays were used to analyze the effect of CelF on SNARE assembly, SNAP29 degradation and ubiquitination, and competitive binding of CelF and PSMD4 to UBQLN1.
RESULTS: CelF depletion severely impaired the metabolic maturation of CCV, suppressed bacterial proliferation in macrophages, and attenuated virulence in vivo. Mechanistically, CelF acted as a molecular decoy that directly bound the ubiquitin-like (UBL) domain of the proteasomal shuttle factor UBQLN1, competitively displacing the proteasome subunit PSMD4. This competitive interference blocked UBQLN1-mediated proteasomal delivery of SNAP29 without altering its ubiquitination status, thereby enhancing SNAP29 protein stability and promoting assembly of the STX17-SNAP29-VAMP8 fusogenic complex. The augmented SNARE activity drove autophagosome-lysosome fusion, sustained autophagic flux, and facilitated lysosomal metabolic remodeling to support CCV biogenesis.
DISCUSSION: Unlike canonical pathogen-encoded UPS modulators that function as E3 ligases or deubiquitinases, CelF operates purely through competitive protein-protein interaction, representing a previously unrecognized paradigm for microbial manipulation of host proteostatic metabolism. Our findings reveal that intracellular pathogens can actively orchestrate organelle metabolic identity by rewiring host proteostasis, and identify the UBQLN1-PSMD4-SNAP29 axis as a novel regulatory checkpoint for SNARE proteostasis and lysosomal metabolic maturation.

title: Coxiella burnetii effector CelF reprograms host proteostasis via competitive disruption of the UBQLN1-PSMD4 axis to stabilize autophagic SNARE SNAP29 and modulate lysosomal metabolic maturation.

abstract: APOBEC3 cytosine deaminases are major sources of cancer mutations. In lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), APOBEC3 activity drives tumor evolution and therapy resistance, nominating these enzymes as therapeutic targets. Although APOBEC3A drives most APOBEC3-associated mutational signature burden across cancers, the relative contributions of individual paralogs in LUAD remain unclear. Here, we define the roles of endogenously misregulated APOBEC3 deaminases using CRISPR-Cas9 knockouts and whole-genome sequencing of 197 long-term propagated single-cell clones. APOBEC3 mutagenesis falls into three patterns, driven predominantly by APOBEC3A, by both APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B, or minimal despite detectable enzyme expression. Commonly used surrogate measures, including mRNA and protein levels and in vitro deaminase activity, do not predict these contributions. We also provide the first causal evidence that endogenous APOBEC3A generates the indel signature InD9a, linking it to uracil excision following cytosine deamination. These heterogeneous contributions highlight the need for biomarkers that resolve individual APOBEC3 activities to guide therapeutic targeting.

title: Heterogeneous contributions of APOBEC3 deaminases to substitution and indel mutagenesis in lung adenocarcinoma.

abstract: RNA viruses encode multiple layers of information within a single molecule, which functions simultaneously as a template for protein synthesis and as a structured regulatory RNA. These structures control key aspects of viral gene expression, govern host interactions, and mediate immune evasion. Although the prevalence of RNA structure in viral genomes is now well established, only recently have functional and mechanistic studies begun to uncover how these elements act as regulatory modules that shape infection outcomes. With their compact genomes and experimentally tractable life cycles, RNA viruses represent powerful model systems for uncovering the fundamental building blocks of riboregulation and illuminating principles of gene control conserved across eukaryotes. Here, we review current mechanistic understanding of RNA structure-based regulation across diverse viral families and draw parallels to structure-mediated gene control in eukaryotic transcriptomes, highlighting RNA structure as a central regulatory layer in gene expression with broad therapeutic and synthetic biology potential.

title: Small genomes, big lessons: What viruses teach us about structure-based riboregulation.

abstract: Alternative splicing (AS) generates distinct mRNA isoforms, and frequently distinct proteins, from single genes; its dysregulation is established in cancer, neurodegeneration, and immune disease. Sequencing now nominates candidate splice events at scale, but a nominated event does not become a usable measurement until an isoform-discriminating sequence has been converted into a physical signal. Existing AS reviews concentrate on sequencing workflows, computational event calling, or disease catalogs; the assay-engineering step that follows target nomination remains comparatively underserved, and it is where most translational failures occur. This review addresses that gap. We group postsequencing detection into five classes defined by the physical origin of the signal: (i) fixed-tissue in situ localization, (ii) live-cell RNA imaging, (iii) plasmonic and spectroscopic readouts, (iv) label-free nanophotonic biosensing combined with site-specific RNA processing, and (v) protein-level proteogenomic confirmation. These classes are compared on target definition, reported analytical performance, multiplexing, matrix compatibility, perturbation risk, and clinical readiness. The reported performance spans single-copy imaging of splice variants in living cells to label-free detection at 580 fM in under 30 min without cDNA synthesis or PCR. Three conclusions follow. First, assay selection should be governed by the class of claim being made rather than by platform novelty. Second, analytical sensitivity measured on synthetic targets systematically overstates readiness in clinical matrices; therefore, matrix-matched validation is not optional. Third, cross-laboratory comparison is currently obstructed by inconsistent reporting, which we address by proposing a minimum performance-reporting set and explicit platform-selection criteria. We close with emerging directions, including CRISPR-based isoform detection, biosensor integration with nanopore sequencing, AI-assisted probe design, and digital and microfluidic formats.
