title: Nanoimaging, Spectroscopy, and Biosensor Assays for Alternatively Spliced RNA Isoforms in Disease Diagnostics.

abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Hypertension remains the leading modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular morbidity and mortality worldwide, yet blood pressure control rates remain suboptimal despite the widespread availability of effective antihypertensive therapies. Poor long-term adherence, therapeutic inertia, and the need for lifelong daily treatment continue to limit the effectiveness of current pharmacological strategies. This review examines the biological rationale, available clinical evidence, and potential role of long-acting RNA-based therapies targeting hepatic angiotensinogen synthesis in hypertension.
RECENT FINDINGS: Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) and antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting angiotensinogen represent a novel therapeutic approach that suppresses production of the unique precursor of the renin-angiotensin system. Zilebesiran has demonstrated sustained reductions in circulating angiotensinogen and ambulatory blood pressure following infrequent subcutaneous administration in phase 1 and phase 2 clinical trials. Antisense strategies have provided additional clinical validation of sustained angiotensinogen inhibition, although their antihypertensive efficacy has been less consistent. Ongoing clinical development is addressing long-term cardiovascular outcomes, safety, and optimal patient selection. RNA-based antihypertensive therapies may represent an important evolution in hypertension management by combining upstream renin-angiotensin system inhibition with prolonged pharmacological activity and reduced dependence on daily medication adherence. However, their future clinical role will depend on evidence regarding long-term safety, cardiovascular outcomes, reversibility, cost-effectiveness, patient selection, and integration with conventional antihypertensive therapy.

abstract: N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc)-modified extracellular vesicles (EVs) derived from hypoxic pancreatic cancer cells and loaded with annexin A2 (ANXA2) small interfering RNA (siRNA) were developed to modulate the immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment (TME). Characterisation confirmed successful surface modification and efficient siRNA loading in EVs with a diameter of approximately 100-120 nm. In vitro, these engineered EVs inhibited pancreatic cancer cell proliferation, migration and invasion and promoted apoptosis. Additional cargo-matched comparison showed that GalNAc-modified hypoxic EVs carrying ANXA2 siRNA produced stronger ANXA2 silencing and more pronounced anti-migratory, anti-invasive and pro-apoptotic effects than unmodified hypoxic EVs carrying the same siRNA. In a xenograft model, treatment suppressed tumour growth and improved survival. Multi-omics and immune analyses suggested suppression of the PI3K/AKT signalling pathway and remodelling of the immunosuppressive TME, as reflected by increased CD8+ T-cell infiltration, reduced tissue-associated immunoreactivity for interleukin-6 (IL-6), interleukin-10 (IL-10), and tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), and increased soluble interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), interleukin-2 (IL-2) and GM-CSF levels. These findings indicate that GalNAc-modified hypoxic EVs carrying ANXA2 siRNA can inhibit tumour progression and modulate the TME in pancreatic cancer, supporting their potential as a therapeutic delivery platform.

abstract: Delivery of CRISPR-Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) using synthetic materials can bypass the host translational machinery and limit the duration of genomic exposure, minimizing the risk of off-target mutations. Despite their advantages, lipid nanoparticle (LNP) platforms for CRISPR-Cas9 RNP delivery that achieve highly efficient editing at low doses remain limited. In the present study, we developed a library of ionizable lipids (ILs) and corresponding LNPs to enhance the delivery and editing efficiencies of CRISPR-Cas9 RNP complexes. Following comprehensive in vitro screening and formulation optimization, an optimal LNP candidate containing the C12A9 IL (denoted as LNPC12A9) was identified that achieved ∼90% EGFP disruption in HEK293T-EGFP cells at an RNP concentration of 30 nM and ∼60% at 15 nM. The editing performance was consistently observed at an RNP concentration of 15 nM when editing the Gcgr and HPRT1 genes across multiple hepatic cell lines. Moreover, coencapsulation of RNP and a single-stranded oligodeoxynucleotide (ssODN) template for homology-directed repair (HDR) within LNPC12A9 induced an HDR rate of 37.8%. Systemic administration of LNPC12A9 into C57BL/6J mice led to liver tropism and a total hepatic Pcsk9 gene disruption rate of 1.39%. In conclusion, this study provides insights into the construction of an LNP platform to improve the delivery efficiency of CRISPR-Cas9 RNP, thereby facilitating the development of LNPs for safe, precise, and tissue-specific Cas9 RNP-based genome editing therapies.

abstract: Gene therapy and RNA-based therapeutics are increasingly limited by the challenge of delivering fragile, anionic nucleic acids to the correct intracellular compartment. Zein, the principal maize prolamin, has attracted interest as a biodegradable, self-assembling carrier that can protect cargo and be combined with polymeric, lipidic, targeted and biomimetic components. This review critically evaluates zein-based systems for plasmid DNA, siRNA, antisense oligonucleotides and related nucleic-acid cargos. Native zein is best regarded as a protective and sustained-release matrix rather than a stand-alone high-efficiency transfection vector. In contrast, hybrid systems can add nucleic-acid condensation, colloidal stabilization, targeting and intracellular-trafficking functions through components such as chitosan, polyethylenimine, dendritic poly(l-lysine), lipids and targeting ligands. Direct evidence of endosomal escape remains limited, with only one reviewed study providing imaging evidence consistent with improved lysosomal escape. Cargo-specific evidence is strongest for plasmid DNA, with functional proof-of-concept also reported for selected siRNA and antisense oligonucleotide systems, whereas robust mRNA translation and CRISPR genome editing have not yet been demonstrated with zein-based carriers. The translational rationale for zein lies not in superior intrinsic transfection efficiency, but in route-specific protection, sustained release, hydrophobic drug co-loading and use as a biodegradable scaffold within multifunctional hybrids. Zein-based gene delivery remains preclinical and requires stronger mechanistic, cargo-specific and route-specific validation.

abstract: Adenosine-to-inosine RNA editing mediated by endogenous ADAR enzymes represents a promising therapeutic strategy because it can correct mutations at the transcript level without inducing permanent changes to the genome. However, existing systems face challenges, particularly the limited editing efficiency, which limits their practical applications. Here we introduce MARRS (multivalent ADAR1-recruiting RNA editing system)-an efficient and specific RNA editing platform that leverages engineered multivalent RNA aptamers to robustly recruit endogenous ADAR1 enzymes. By optimizing aptamers targeting the Zα domain of ADAR1 p150 and embedding them in a circular RNA scaffold, MARRS enables near-complete adenosine-to-inosine editing of RNA targets in cultured cells and mouse models, achieving efficiencies up to 100% in vitro and 84% in vivo. MARRS also exhibits remarkable versatility across a range of transcript targets while maintaining high specificity with minimal off-target effects. Operating without the need for exogenous enzymes, the MARRS system offers a safe, efficient and programmable platform.

title: Aptamer-mediated multivalent endogenous ADAR1 recruitment for highly efficient RNA editing.

abstract: Viral infections represent a major global health challenge due to the rapid emergence of new pathogens, increasing antiviral drug resistance and limited efficacy of traditional treatments against evolving viruses. Nanotechnology is a promising interdisciplinary approach to fighting viral diseases, which can perform direct viral inactivation, targeted drug delivery, immune modulation, vaccine development, rapid diagnostics, and prevention of infection. This review offers an in-depth and critical overview of the major antiviral nanoparticle platforms, including metallic, metal oxide, carbon-based, polymeric, lipid-based, and bio-inspired nanoparticles. In this article, we employ a comparative framework to systematically analyze classes of nanoparticles based on their physicochemical properties, molecular mechanisms of antiviral action, biomedical applications, and translational potential. Antiviral mechanisms are discussed within the framework of the viral life cycle, including the inhibition of viral attachment and entry, destruction of viral envelope and capsid integrity, suppression of intracellular viral replication, reactive oxygen species-mediated viral inactivation, immune-modulation, and nanoparticle-assisted therapeutic delivery. Moreover, the review critically discusses the increasing biomedical applications of antiviral nanoparticles in therapeutics, vaccine delivery, diagnostics, antiviral coatings, gene therapy and precision nanomedicine, while highlighting the clinically successful technologies such as lipid nanoparticle-based mRNA vaccines. Special attention is paid to the main obstacles in clinical translation, such as nanotoxicity, biodistribution, manufacturing scalability, regulatory challenges, and the lack of standard evaluation protocols. Finally, major knowledge gaps and future research priorities are highlighted, focusing on the design of multifunctional, clinically translatable and regulatory-compliant nanoplatforms. This review offers insights on antiviral nanomedicines and practical insights for the rational design and successful clinical translation of next-generation antiviral nanoparticle.

title: Antiviral nanoparticles: mechanisms, biomedical applications and clinical translation toward next-generation therapies.

abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-based immunotherapy has transformed cancer treatment by enabling engineered immune cells to selectively recognize and eliminate malignant targets, with CAR-T cells establishing the first major clinical success in this field. However, severe associated toxicities, logistical complexities of autologous manufacturing, and high rates of antigen-loss relapse have accelerated the development of alternative effector platforms such as CAR-NK cells. CAR-NK cells combine antigen-directed cytotoxicity with the innate antitumor functions of natural killer cells, offering a potentially safer and more readily available off-the-shelf therapeutic strategy. Nevertheless, the clinical efficacy of CAR-NK therapy is constrained by key biological and translational hurdles: brief in vivo persistence, inadequate trafficking and solid tumor infiltration, severe susceptibility to tumor microenvironment-mediated immunosuppression, and antigen escape driven by tumor heterogeneity. These biological constraints are compounded by technical bottlenecks, including cell source variability, limited large-scale expansion capacity, ex vivo functional exhaustion, and an absence of standardized manufacturing protocols. To address these multi-faceted barriers, recent advances in genome engineering, systems biology, and computational modeling provide promising routes forward. Given that prolonged exposure to immunosuppressive niches induces functional impairment, genome-editing strategies targeting inhibitory checkpoints and persistence programs are crucial; however, enhancing persistence requires stringent safeguards to mitigate toxicity risks from constitutive signaling or genomic instability. Thus, engineering next-generation CAR-NK cells necessitates balancing extended longevity, potent cytotoxicity, and safety. Multiomics approaches facilitate deeper characterization of CAR-NK functional states and tumor-immune interactions, whereas artificial intelligence-guided engineering integrates high-dimensional biological and manufacturing data to optimize receptor design, predict therapeutic performance, and accelerate translational workflows. Collectively, these innovations support a paradigm shift toward programmable CAR-NK cells that can dynamically sense, adapt, and respond to tumor evolution, driving the transition toward autonomous, highly scalable, and precisely controllable cellular immunotherapies in precision oncology.

abstract: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by antibody-mediated platelet destruction and impaired regulatory T-cell (Treg) function, yet its molecular basis remains poorly defined. Here, we show that CD4+ naive T cells from patients with ITP exhibit diminished T-cell receptor (TCR) signaling and impaired in vitro Treg induction relative to healthy controls. RNA sequencing revealed widespread dysregulation of alternative splicing, most notably exon 8 skipping in LCK, a kinase central to TCR signaling and Treg differentiation. Using an LCK minigene combined with RNA pull-down mass spectrometry and RNA immunoprecipitation assays, we identified the splicing factor SRSF1 as a direct upstream regulator of LCK exon 8 skipping. Notably, SRSF1 expression was reduced in CD4+ naive T cells from patients with ITP, and its overexpression restored in vitro Treg induction capacity. Antisense oligonucleotide-mediated blockade of SRSF1 binding to LCK enhanced exon 8 skipping and attenuated TCR activation in Jurkat cells. Although murine Lck lacks the human-specific recursive splicing sites required for exon 8 exclusion, the adoptive transfer of CD4+ naive T cells expressing the exon 8-skipped murine Lck into CD61-knockout mice significantly reduced Treg proportions and platelet counts in an active ITP model. Mechanistically, Jurkat cells engineered to express only the exon 8-skipped LCK variant showed markedly reduced binding to ZAP70 and CD3ζ, which may partly account for the attenuated TCR signaling and downstream FOXP3 induction. Together, these findings define a novel SRSF1-LCK splicing axis that may regulate Treg development in ITP.

title: Reduced SRSF1 expression correlates with LCK exon skipping and impaired Treg induction in immune thrombocytopenia.

abstract: Group A Streptococcus (GAS), or Streptococcus pyogenes, causes a connected spectrum of pharyngeal, cutaneous, invasive and immune-mediated diseases. Although beta-lactams remain active, treatment alone has not controlled transmission, recurrent infection, rapid invasive progression or acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease. Control is further weakened by increased macrolide and clindamycin resistance, heterogeneous diagnostic access, asymptomatic carriage, crowded living conditions and unreliable continuity of secondary prophylaxis. These limitations have shifted the field from a predominantly treatment-centered approach toward the development of vaccines as a prevention strategy. Target selection is guided by virulence functions that are required for colonization, immune evasion and tissue injury. These include the M protein, group A carbohydrate (GAC), streptolysin O, Streptococcus pyogenes cell envelope protease (SpyCEP), Streptococcus pyogenes adhesion and division protein (SpyAD), C5a peptidase and other conserved surface or secreted antigens. Current strategies include multivalent type-specific M-protein vaccines, conserved M-protein peptide vaccines, glycoconjugates, multicomponent non-M-protein formulations and mRNA-lipid nanoparticle platforms. The clinical pipeline has recently broadened. Phase I studies have been completed for StreptAnova and MJ8VAX, whereas the J8-K4S2 and p*17-K4S2 clinical trial studies have been completed, with peer-reviewed results pending. The GSK four-component vaccine initiated phase I evaluation in 2025 and remained under clinical evaluation in 2026, whereas the VAX-A1 formulation entered a first-in-human phase I study in 2026. However, no licensed GAS vaccine is available. Progress remains constrained by uncertain correlates of protection, autoimmune safety requirements, geographical emm diversity, endpoint selection and the need for trials in high-burden populations. This narrative review therefore focuses on the disease problem, targetable virulence mechanisms, limits of antimicrobial control, current vaccine pipeline and interventions required to complement future vaccine use.

abstract: Since the discovery of the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat (CRISPR)-associated (Cas) system, genome-editing technologies have advanced rapidly, and the field has expanded substantially. In parallel, artificial intelligence (AI) has progressed at an unprecedented pace and is transforming genetic engineering. Early AI applications primarily addressed predictive tasks, including guide RNA (gRNA) activity, off-target effects, and editing outcomes for CRISPR-Cas nucleases, base editors, and prime editors. Recently, transformer-based protein language models (PLMs) and generative AI have expanded the role of AI beyond prediction to direct molecular design. Thus, AI-driven frameworks can now evolve genome-editing proteins, design molecular architectures, and generate de novo genome-editing enzymes. This review discusses how AI is reshaping genome engineering, from gRNA activity prediction to the design of next-generation editors.

abstract: R2 retroelements are non-long-terminal-repeat retrotransposons that primarily insert into 28S ribosomal DNA loci across diverse eukaryotes. R2 elements home to their target sites through target-primed reverse transcription (TPRT), in which the R2 protein recognizes and nicks the target DNA to prime reverse transcription using an R2-encoding RNA as the template. The avian R2 system from Taeniopygia guttata (R2Tg) can insert a payload sequence within an RNA template into 28S ribosomal DNA loci in human cells. Here, we present cryo-electron microscopy structures of the R2Tg-template RNA-target DNA complex in the TPRT initiation state, both alone and bound to a Cas9-guide RNA complex. These structures provide mechanistic insights into R2Tg-mediated TPRT in its natural context and in the programmable gene integration system STITCHR (site-specific target-primed insertion through targeted CRISPR homing of retroelements). Furthermore, we combine these structural insights with computational protein design methods to engineer an enhanced STITCHR system.

abstract: The voltage-gated sodium channel NaV1.7 (SCN9A) is a genetically validated target for pain therapy, but achieving therapeutic isoform selectivity remains a formidable challenge for small-molecule inhibitors. Here, we overcome this bottleneck through a highly selective RNA-targeted strategy that dictates SCN9A alternative splicing. We first identified ASO50 as the most potent baseline candidate antisense oligonucleotide (ASO). Subsequent 5'-decoy (5D) sequence screening yielded an upgraded candidate, L9C-ASO50, which is engineered to competitively intercept U1 snRNA, achieving a cooperative spatial hindrance that robustly suppresses exon 5 recognition. This targeted exon exclusion introduces a frameshift that triggers robust, obligate transcript clearance via the nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) pathway, ensuring complete functional silencing without cross-reacting with homologous NaV channels. Mechanistically, we define the underlying cis-trans regulatory architecture, revealing a homeostatic tug-of-war where the RNA-binding protein ELAVL2 enforces exon inclusion, paradoxically antagonized by the canonical SR protein family. Crucially, CNS-restricted delivery of L9C-ASO50 produces profound and sustained mechanical and thermal analgesia. These findings establish splice-modulated transcript degradation as a viable therapeutic paradigm for chronic pain and provide a broadly applicable blueprint for engineering targeted RNA therapeutics.

abstract: The bacterium Rhodococcus equi is a common cause of severe pneumonia in foals worldwide. Foals are exposed to R. equi from birth and are most susceptible in the first weeks of life. In North America, control measures are limited to transfusion to newborn foals of hyperimmune plasma whose potency is assessed by surpassing a threshold of IgG against the virulence-associated protein A (VapA) of R. equi. Here we report results of vaccination of pregnant mares with mRNA encoding a GPI-anchored virulence-associated protein A (VapA) of R. equi induced VapA-specific IgG subisotypes transferred to their foals during the 63-day period after birth. Pregnant mares were randomly assigned to receive either VapA mRNA vaccine (n=10) at 8 and 10 months of gestation or no vaccine (n=10). Serum was collected from mares at 8 months of gestation (before vaccination for immunized mares) and {approx}24 hours after foaling and from foals at ages 1, 35, and 63 days. Mean relative concentrations of were low before immunization in all mares and did not change over time in unvaccinated mares; however, mean relative concentrations of anti-VapA IgG1, IgG4/7, and IgG3/5 of mares were significantly increased after VapA mRNA immunization and strongly correlated with the corresponding concentrations in their foals sera at age {approx}24 hours. Concentrations of anti-VapA IgGs remained increased in foals of vaccinated mares compared with control foals for at least 35 days.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: RNA editing is an epitranscriptomic mechanism that shapes transcriptome diversity and fine-tunes neuronal function. While adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) editing by ADAR enzymes has been extensively studied in neurodegenerative disorders, the role of cytidine-to-uridine (C-to-U) editing catalyzed by APOBEC1 remains largely unexplored.
METHODS: We investigated the impact of APOBEC1 on RNA editing homeostasis and prion disease progression using complementary in vitro and in vivo models. Global RNA editing and gene expression profiles were established in non-infected N2A and prion-infected sc-N2A murine neuroblastoma cells, under control conditions or following APOBEC1 depletion. APOBEC1 was silenced by shRNA-mediated knockdown to assess its regulatory contribution. In vivo disease progression was assessed in Apobec1 knockout mice subjected to RML prion infection to evaluate survival outcomes.
RESULTS: Prion infection was associated with a global increase in RNA editing and an expanded repertoire of edited transcripts in sc-N2A cells. APOBEC1 depletion markedly reduced the overall editing levels, affecting both A-to-I and C-to-U editing events, reshaping editing patterns in transcripts associated with RNA and protein transport, cellular stress responses, synaptic signaling, and neuroimmune interactions. Consistently, Apobec1 KO mice exhibited accelerated body weight loss and significantly shortened survival following RML prion challenge.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings support APOBEC1 as a contributor to RNA editing homeostasis and suggest that APOBEC1 loss reduces resilience to prion-induced neurodegenerative stress. APOBEC1 deficiency was associated with altered editome profiles in prion-infected cells and accelerated disease progression in the RML prion model.

abstract: Guanidine-bridged nucleic acid (GuNA) is a bridged nucleic acid analog with high binding affinity toward complementary strands along with high nuclease resistance. GuNA has been developed to improve pharmacokinetics and safety profiles of phosphorothioate modified gapmers. Here, we evaluated antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) modified with combination of GuNA and 2'-O-methoxyethyl (MOE) and found that the dual-modification strategy could significantly improve knockdown activity in vitro and in vivo. Long-term efficacy evaluation showed that intracerebroventricularly administered GuNA-modified gapmers stayed active for over 24 weeks in mouse brain. Furthermore, we observed that GuNA-modified gapmers could evade lymphocyte-derived immune responses and kept ASO-induced toxicity in check. Taken together, the results of this study demonstrate that GuNA modification can improve the functional potential of ASOs, especially in the central nervous system.

abstract: The goal of this clinical trial is to test if the drug SKY-0515, an oral medication, can lower harmful proteins linked to Huntington's Disease (HD) and improve the symptoms of participants with HD. This study includes men and women aged 25 and older who have HD confirmed by genetic testing and meet certain requirements for physical ability and independence.
description: This study is a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial conducted across multiple sites. This clinical trial aims to evaluate the safety, pharmacodynamics, and efficacy of SKY-0515, a novel, orally administered small molecule. Huntington's Disease (HD) is a rare, inherited neurodegenerative condition caused by a mutation in the huntingtin (HTT) gene, resulting in excessive production of mutant huntingtin (mHTT) protein, which damages nerve cells and leads to progressive motor, cognitive, and psychiatric symptoms. SKY-0515 is designed to reduce mHTT protein levels, leading to a decrease in both wild-type and mutant forms of HTT protein. Additionally, the drug lowers postmeiotic segregation 1 (PMS1) protein, which plays a role in somatic CAG repeat expansion-a key driver of HD progression. Participants must be aged 25 or older, have genetically confirmed HD (CAG repeat length ≥ 40), and meet specific functional and motor criteria. They will be assigned randomly to one of four treatment arms (three doses of SKY-0515 and one placebo group). Safety and efficacy will be evaluated through blood tests, imaging (MRI), and clinical assessments, including the Unified Huntington's Disease Rating Scale (UHDRS).

outcomes.description: cUHDRS includes the Total Functional Capacity (range, 0-13; higher score means better functioning), Total Motor Score (range, 0-124; higher score means worse motor severity), Symbol Digit Modality Test (range, 0-110, correctly paired numbers-symbols in 90 seconds; higher score means better cognitive performance), and Stroop Color and Word Test (range, 0-no max value, correctly read color words in 45 seconds; higher score means better cognitive performance) scores. A z-score for each test is calculated, which alone can be used to describe relationship between an individual's test score and the mean score of a target population. A z-score of 0 is the mean, and ±1 is 1 standard deviation from the mean. For cUHDRS, z-scores of each test are summed, whereby a higher cUHDRS score is better (score of -3.06-no max value) and a change of ≥1.2 is a meaningful worsening, shown to track functional decline.
outcomes.measure: Change From Baseline in the Z-score from the Composite Unified Huntington's Disease Rating Scale (cUHDRS)

outcomes.description: The total motor score (TMS) assessed motor features of HD with standardized ratings of oculomotor function, dysarthria, chorea, dystonia, gait, and postural stability. Some items (such as chorea and dystonia) required grading each extremity (face, bucco-oral-lingual, and trunk) separately. Eye movements require both horizontal and vertical grades. The total motor impairment score is the sum of all the individual 31 motor sub-items (each rated from 0 to 4), with higher scores indicating more severe motor impairment than lower scores. The range of TMS is 0-124.
outcomes.measure: Change from Baseline in Total Motor Score (TMS)

outcomes.description: TFC consists of five ordinally scaled items assessing a person's capacity with: (1) occupation; (2) financial affairs; (3) domestic responsibilities; (4) activities of daily living; and (5) independent living. Total score ranges from zero (worst) to 13 (best).
outcomes.measure: Change from Baseline in Total Functional Capacity (TFC)

outcomes.description: The independence scale assesses independence on a 0 to 100 scale with higher scores indicating better functioning.
outcomes.measure: Change from Baseline in Independence Scale Score (IS)

outcomes.description: The SDMT assesses attention, visuoperceptual processing, working memory, and cognitive/psychomotor speed. The score is the number of correctly paired abstract symbols and specific numbers in 90 seconds with higher scores indicating better cognitive functioning.
outcomes.measure: Change from Baseline in Symbol Digit Modalities Test (SDMT)

outcomes.description: In the Stroop Color and Word Test (SCWT) the number of words and colors read correctly is counted, with a higher score indicating better cognitive performance scores. There is no upper limit for SWR as it is a time-based task. The lower limit (worst possible) however is 0; higher score is better meaning less severity.
outcomes.measure: Change from Baseline in the Stroop Color and Word Test (SCWT)

abstract:
MOTIVATION: The interaction between RNA and proteins is a complex process that involves atom-level details and dynamic changes. Accurate prediction of protein-RNA interactions helps researchers to develop protein-targeted small nucleic acid drugs. However, the scarcity of protein-RNA complexes and experimental data limits the ability of existing data-driven supervised learning methods to learn latent patterns, leading to limited performance.
RESULTS: In this study, we propose PRIDA (Protein-RNA Interaction prediction based on Domain-Adversarial learning), a protein-RNA interaction framework that combines bilinear attention with conditional domain-adversarial learning. Powered by pretrained protein and RNA language models, PRIDA improves interaction prediction under protein-level distribution shifts and limited labeled data. By integrating PRIDA with Monte Carlo Tree Search, we apply it to a virtual screening pipeline to generate RNA aptamer candidates for specific target proteins. Experimental results show that PRIDA achieves state-of-the-art performance in cross-domain protein-RNA interaction prediction and provides effective guidance for RNA aptamer virtual screening.
AVAILABILITY: The data and source code of the proposed method are available at GitHub (https://github.com/zhouyyang/PRIDA) and Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/records/23644677).
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

abstract: This study will evaluate 2 dose levels of mRNA-1283 in participants ≥6 months to \<12 years to determine the optimal dose level per age group.
description:
mRNA-1283 will be administered at 2 different dose levels (Dose Level 1 and Dose Level 2), with mRNA-1273 serving as the active comparator. Dose Level 1 will be the lower dose, and Dose Level 2 will be the higher dose.

The study will consist of 2 cohorts. In Cohort 1, mRNA-1283 will be administered as a single dose to participants aged ≥2 to \<12 years, regardless of prior coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) vaccination status, with mRNA-1273 included as a comparator. In Cohort 2, mRNA-1283 will be administered as a 2-dose series to participants aged ≥6 months to \<2 years who are previously unvaccinated for COVID-19, with mRNA-1273 included as a comparator.

abstract:
Background:

CGD is caused by a gene mutation. For people with CGD, their cells cannot kill germs well, so they can get frequent or life-threatening infections. Researchers want to see if a new procedure can help a person s cells kill germs for a short time. It uses messenger RNA (mRNA) to deliver correct instructions for the gene mutation to the cells.

Objective:

To test a procedure in which mRNA is added to a person s blood cells.

Eligibility:

Males aged 18-75 with CGD with a mutation in the gene that makes the protein gp91phox.

Design:

Participants will be screened with:

Medical history

Physical exam

Blood and urine tests

Swab to test for strep throat

Some screening tests will be repeated during the study.

Participants will be admitted to the NIH Clinical Center hospital for at least 7 days. They will have apheresis. For this, a medicine is injected under their skin to prepare their white blood cells for collection. An IV line is placed into an arm vein. Blood goes through the IV line into a machine that divides whole blood into red blood cells, plasma, and white blood cells. The white blood cells are removed, and the rest of the blood is returned to the participant through an IV line in their other arm. The next day, they will get their mRNA-corrected cells via IV. They will be monitored for 3 more days.

After discharge, participants will keep a symptom diary. They will be contacted weekly for one month, and then once a month. They will have a follow-up visit 3 months after the infusion....

description:
Study Design:

This is a phase 1, open-label, dose-escalation trial to assess the safety and feasibility of administering CGD-Grans to adult patients with X-linked CGD and to identify the maximum tolerated dose (MTD). Subjects will undergo granulocyte-enriched apheresis to provide cell product for mRNA-correction and then receive 1 administration of study agent. The first subjects enrolled will receive the study agent at the lowest dose, and when a level has been determined to be safe, the dose level will be increased to a second and then third dose level for subsequent subjects.Subjects will be hospitalized for at least 3 days after study agent administration and will return for a final study visit about 3 months after administration. Blood will be collected regularly for safety and research evaluations. The study hypothesis is that it is safe and feasible to administer mRNA-transfected autologous granulocyte-enriched apheresis product to restore protein expression and phagocyte nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase function in patients with CGD.

Study Agent Description:

The study agent is one administration of autologous CGD mRNA transfected granulocyte-enriched cells, referred to as CGD-Grans. The study agent is derived from apheresis product enriched for granulocytes, which are then transfected with CGD mRNA and administered as an intravenous (IV) infusion. CGD-Grans will be evaluated using the 3+3 modified Fibonacci model at the following 3 escalating dosages:

Dose K: 1 x 10\^6 granulocyte-enriched cells/kg body mass

Dose K+1: 1 x 10\^7 granulocyte-enriched cells/kg body mass

Dose K+2: 1-5 x 10\^8 granulocyte-enriched cells/kg body mass

Each dose will be evaluated in at least 3 subjects. Dose escalation will be managed by a predetermined algorithm depending on the occurrence of drug-related toxicity (DRT). There will be at least 1 week between study agent administration to each subject.

Primary Objectives:

1. Determine the safety and feasibility of CGD-Grans infusion.
2. Determine an MTD for administration.

Secondary Objectives:

1. Assess efficacy of CGD-Grans at restoring NADPH oxidase.
2. Determine the kinetics of CGD-Grans.

Exploratory Objectives:

1. Assess for inflammatory responses to CGD-Grans infusion.
2. Assess for immune responses to protein expressed by the transfected mRNA.
3. Evaluate in vitro bactericidal activity of CGD-Grans.

Primary Endpoints:

1. Determine safety and feasibility by:

   Safety: Frequency of grade 3 or greater adverse events (AEs) or serious adverse events (SAEs) related to the study agent.

   Feasibility: Recruitment, implementation, and manufacturing of CGD-Grans for infusions.
2. MTD determination based on the rate of AEs. MTD is defined as the highest dose level that does not cause the same grade 3 or 4 AEs in 3 or more patients.

Secondary Endpoints:

1. Determine percent of circulating dihydrorhodamine (DHR) positive granulocytes following study agent infusion.
2. Serial measurement of circulating DHR+ granulocytes from peripheral blood until day 3 following study agent infusion or disappearance of DHR+ granulocytes.

Exploratory Endpoint:

1. Assess for increased expression of inflammation-related genes after study agent infusion.
2. Evaluate for development of antibodies against mRNA-expressed CGDphox.
3. Perform in vitro bactericidal activity of CGD-Grans.

abstract: The goal of this study is to determine the safety and antitumor effects of REM-422, a MYB mRNA degrader, in people with Higher Risk MDS and relapsed/refractory AML
description:
This is a Phase 1, open-label, non-randomized, multicenter study investigating REM-422, a potent, selective, and oral small molecule mRNA degrader that reduces expression of the MYB transcription factor for patients with higher risk MDS or relapsed/refractory AML.

This study includes a Dose Escalation Phase and a Dose Expansion Phase. The purpose of the Dose Escalation Phase is to determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and/or recommended Phase 2 dose (RP2D) of REM-422 in patients with higher risk MDS or relapsed/refractory AML. The purpose of Dose Expansion is to further evaluate the safety and anti-tumor activity of the RP2D carried forward from Dose Escalation.

Participation in this study will continue until disease progression, therapy intolerance, or participant withdrawal.

description:
This study is an open-label, two-arm, multi-step phase I study evaluating a combination of two broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs), VRC07-523LS and PGT121.414.LS, in people living with HIV (PWH) who started antiretroviral therapy (ART) during acute/early infection. Participants will receive PGT121.414.LS and VRC07-523LS prior to undergoing an analytical treatment interruption (ATI). Participants will restart ART and continue follow-up after ATI to confirm viral suppression.

Participants will be screened for eligibility and have a pre-entry visit. After determination of eligibility, participants will be enrolled sequentially into Arm A (n=20) and then Arm B (n=20). The study consists of three steps including an analytic treatment interruption.

Arm A:

* Step 1: Participants remain on ART and will receive an infusion of VRC07-523LS and PGT121.414.LS at study entry.
* Step 2: Participants will interrupt their ART and receive a second infusion of VRC07-523LS 12 weeks after the initial infusion. Participants will be monitored closely for indications to resume ART.
* Step 3: Upon meeting ART restart criteria in Step 2; participants will resume ART and be followed for up to 24 weeks.

Arm B:

* Step 1: Participants remain on ART and will receive an infusion of VRC07-523LS and PGT121.414.LS at study entry and a second infusion of VRC07-523LS 12 weeks later.
* Step 2: Participants will interrupt their ART. Participants will be monitored closely for indications to resume ART.
* Step 3: Upon meeting ART restart criteria in Step 2; participants will resume ART and be followed for up to 24 weeks.

Participation in both arms will last up to 98 weeks.

abstract: mRNA-lipid nanoparticles (mRNA-LNPs) have revolutionized nucleic acid therapeutics, yet their clinical success relies heavily on precise manufacturing processes. This review comprehensively explores the critical intersection between microfluidic channel design, lipid self-assembly biophysics, and the subsequent biological performance of mRNA-LNPs. First, we analyze the fundamental fluid mechanics driving representative microfluidic mixers, elucidating how different channel architectures dictate solvent exchange rates and nanoparticle assembly kinetics. We then systematically examine how these specific mixing regimes modulate essential physicochemical characteristics, including lipid distribution, internal nanostructure, particle morphology, size distribution, and overall colloidal stability. Crucially, we bridge the gap between manufacturing and pharmacology by evaluating how mixing-induced physicochemical differences directly translate into distinct biological outcomes, such as cellular uptake mechanisms, endosomal escape efficiency, and systemic pharmacokinetics. By integrating microfluidic engineering principles with biological evaluation, this review provides a mechanistic framework for understanding how continuous-flow assembly processes program the functional behavior of mRNA-LNP systems. Ultimately, we highlight emerging design principles essential for developing the next generation of robust, highly efficient nucleic acid delivery platforms.

abstract: mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines can elicit robust T cell responses; however, these responses remain insufficient, particularly in the context of cancer vaccine therapy. Although several types of adjuvants reportedly enhance T cell responses induced by mRNA-LNP vaccines, few comprehensive side-by-side comparisons exist, and it remains unclear which adjuvants are most suitable. Herein, we screened 15 adjuvants. The addition of class B CpG oligodeoxynucleotides (ODNs) markedly augmented T cell induction in an interleukin-12-dependent manner and promoted the antitumor effects of mRNA-LNP vaccines in mice. Class B CpG ODN-adjuvanted mRNA-LNP vaccines induced more potent T cell responses than the mRNA-LNP vaccine administered at a 10-fold higher dose, while exhibiting a more favorable safety profile. However, this approach also reduced the cellular uptake of mRNA-LNPs and antigen expression. As a possible mechanism underlying this reduced delivery efficiency, we found that class B CpG ODNs adsorbed onto LNPs and altered their particle characteristics. These findings demonstrate that supplementation with class B CpG ODN is a simple, safe, and readily implementable approach for enhancing mRNA-LNP vaccine-induced T cell responses. This study also highlights that adding auxiliary components to mRNA-LNPs can potentially affect the performance of LNPs as delivery carriers.

title: Enhancing mRNA-lipid nanoparticle vaccine-induced T cell responses by simple supplementation with class B CpG oligodeoxynucleotides.

abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus has recently emerged in dairy cattle in the USA, leading to mastitis and sharp reductions in milk production. The main site of H5N1 viral replication is the mammary tissue rather than the respiratory tract and viral transmission between animals is thought to occur through viral shedding in milk. Here, we generate an mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (mRNA-LNP) vaccine encoding the hemagglutinin (HA) of A/dairy cattle/Texas/24-008749-002/2024, representative of circulating bovine H5N1 viruses, and assess its immunogenicity and efficacy in lactating dairy cows. Eight cows were divided into vaccinated and control groups, receiving two intramuscular doses of the vaccine or saline, followed by intramammary viral challenge. Vaccination elicited HA-reactive and neutralizing antibodies in serum and HA-reactive antibodies in milk. Following viral challenge, vaccinated cows had ~1,000-fold lower peak viral RNA in milk and a lower occurrence of mastitis and mammary fibrosis.

abstract: The worldwide opioid epidemic continues to claim thousands of lives each year and remains one of the most urgent global public health challenges, driven by the high abuse potential and overdose risk of potent, fully synthetic μ-opioid receptor (MOR) agonists such as fentanyl. While fentanyl is highly effective in pain management, it also carries severe risks including respiratory depression, addiction, and fatal overdose. Understanding the neurobiological pathways underlying these risks is essential for developing safer analgesics and effective interventions. The MOR, a G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) that modulates neuronal excitability and synaptic transmission in important brain circuits like the ventral tegmental area (VTA), nucleus accumbens (NAc), and prefrontal cortex (PFC), is the primary receptor through which opioids exert their therapeutic effects. Dopaminergic dysregulation, transcriptional remodeling, and altered synaptic plasticity are neuroadaptations brought on by long-term opioid exposure that contribute to dependence and relapse. Life-threatening opioid toxicity is primarily driven by MOR-mediated suppression of respiratory networks, with risk shaped by dose, pharmacokinetics, receptor efficacy, and circuit sensitivity. Zebrafish (Danio rerio) provide a powerful complementary system for dissecting opioid-related neurocircuitry and screening for potential therapeutics. Zebrafish share conserved opioid-signaling components with mammals, and larval transparency facilitates in vivo imaging of neuronal activity at cellular resolution. Behavioral paradigms capture reward-related and drug-seeking phenotypes, while CRISPR-based approaches offer a means to investigate receptor-specific functions in validated models. In addition, zebrafish larvae provide an efficient platform for high-throughput screening of compounds that modulate opioid signaling and respiratory-related phenotypes. Together, insights from human, rodent, and zebrafish studies provide a more integrated understanding of opioid overdose and addiction neurobiology. This review incorporates current knowledge on the molecular and circuit-level mechanisms driving these processes and discusses how zebrafish models accelerate the discovery of safer analgesics and novel treatments for opioid use disorder and overdose.

abstract: β-thalassaemia is characterised by ineffective erythropoiesis, chronic anaemia, haemolysis, and progressive iron-related and non-iron-related morbidity. Although transfusion, iron chelation, multidisciplinary care, and allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation have substantially improved outcomes, major gaps persist in treatment burden, access, safety, adherence, and curative feasibility. Over the past decade, the therapeutic landscape has expanded rapidly, with disease-modifying agents targeting erythroid maturation and red cell metabolism, including luspatercept and mitapivat, now available as options for both transfusion-dependent and non-transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia. In parallel, gene addition and gene editing therapies, particularly beti-cel and exa-cel, have established proof of curative potential independent of donor availability. However, optimal patient selection, response definitions, long-term outcome assessment, affordability, and equitable global access remain central challenges for wide implementation. In this Series paper, we discuss advances in β-thalassaemia treatment over the past decade, including newly approved and late-stage therapies and their future implications, and highlight remaining research gaps.

title: The expanding therapeutic landscape of β-thalassaemia.

abstract: Ribosomopathies are a heterogeneous group of rare inherited disorders caused by defects in ribosome biogenesis or function, leading to bone marrow failure (BMF), congenital anomalies, immune dysfunction, and increased risk of malignancy. Ribosomopathies associated with hematological phenotype include Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SDS), Diamond-Blackfan anemia (DBA), and cartilage-hair hypoplasia (CHH). Allogenic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) remains the only curative treatment for the hematologic manifestations of these conditions, although it does not correct their extra-hematologic features. In SDS, HCT is indicated for progressive bone marrow failure, myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), or high-risk clonal evolution. Recent insights into TP53-driven leukemogenesis have improved risk stratification and may support earlier transplantation. Nevertheless, role of TP53 monitoring, timing of HCT, cytoreduction before HCT in MDS/AML, and poor outcomes after leukemic transformation remain major challenges. In DBA, HCT is reserved for transfusion dependence, steroid refractoriness/dependence, BMF, immunodeficiency, or clonal evolution. Outcomes have improved substantially, with recent studies demonstrating comparable survival after matched sibling donor (MSD) and matched unrelated donor (MUD) transplantation. Careful management of iron overload and lifelong cancer surveillance are essential components of care. In CHH, HCT is indicated for severe immunodeficiency, transfusion-dependent anemia, and BMF. Across all ribosomopathies, outcomes are most favorable when transplantation is performed before irreversible organ damage or malignant transformation. Advances in molecular monitoring, particularly for clonal evolution, together with emerging gene therapy and gene-editing approaches, are opening new therapeutic perspectives and may eventually provide alternatives to HCT for selected patients.

abstract: Patients with acute leukemias harboring translocations involving gene lysine methyltransferase 2A (KMT2A) have a poor prognosis due to chemotherapy resistance with rapid relapse following standard treatments. The resulting KMT2A fusion proteins dysregulate gene expression, leading to an upregulation of leukemogenic transcription factors such as HOXA9 and MEIS1, which drives leukemic transformation. Although menin inhibitors are proving to be promising new therapeutics for patients with KMT2A-rearranged (KMT2Ar) acute leukemia, resistance mechanisms have already been described and new therapeutic approaches for this patient subgroup must be identified. Here, a genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screen in a KMT2Ar B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia cell line identified the deubiquitinase ubiquitin-specific peptidase 22 (USP22) as a novel regulator of MEIS1 protein stability. USP22 is a member of the Spt-Ada-Gcn5 acetyltransferase multiprotein complex, which has crucial functions in shaping the chromatin landscape and modulating transcription. Genetic depletion of USP22 impaired cellular growth and proliferation in KMT2Ar acute leukemia models. Chromatin immunoprecipitation revealed cooperative binding between USP22 and MEIS1 at critical oncogenic target genes, suggesting that USP22 safeguards leukemogenic transcription by protecting MEIS1 from proteasomal degradation. Genetic or chemical inhibition of USP22 led to the polyubiquitination of MEIS1, resulting in proteasomal degradation and downregulation of the expression of target genes. Our study identifies USP22 as a novel regulator of MEIS1 protein stability that could potentially be exploited as a therapeutic target in the future in KMT2Ar leukemias.

abstract: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) replication depends on a complex interplay between viral proteins and host cellular factors, which represent promising therapeutic targets. However, systematic integration of results from genome-wide CRISPR screens for HIV host factors remains limited. Here, we performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of pooled genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screens to identify host dependency, restriction, and latency-promoting factors in HIV-1 infection. Following PRISMA guidelines, we identified 11 eligible studies from which we extracted 26 gene lists. These were classified into three phenotypic categories, including dependency (5 lists), restriction (10 lists), and latency-promoting (7 lists), and integrated using meta-analysis by information content (MAIC). GO over-representation analysis and Gene Set Enrichment Analysis were performed on MAIC-ranked gene lists to characterize pathway architectures. MAIC successfully recovered well-established host factors, including the entry receptors CD4, CCR5, and CXCR4; the integration cofactor PSIP1 (LEDGF/p75); and the restriction factors TRIM5, TRIM22, PML, G3BP1, and EIF2AK2. RNF114 emerged as the top-ranked restriction factor, supported by four independent publication-level categories. Additional high-confidence hits included TRIM56, BIRC3, DTX3L, and components of the ubiquitin-proteasome system across the dependency and latency datasets, further supporting the robustness of the MAIC framework. Beyond these canonical factors, we identified multiple undercharacterized genes and pathways, including coagulation and IL-17 signaling in dependency factors, SUMOylation and DNA damage response in restriction factors, and the Integrator complex and proteasome-granule co-enrichment in latency-promoting factors. Leading-edge analysis confirmed that most of these non-canonical enrichments are driven by coherent gene modules rather than a small set of pleiotropic hubs. These findings reveal distinct pathway architectures across the three infection states and highlight previously unrecognized host processes that may serve as targets for antiviral therapy. Our analysis provides a comprehensive resource for guiding future mechanistic studies of host-HIV interactions and developing strategies to enhance immunity, block viral replication, and reverse latency.

abstract: Bacterial extracellular vesicles (BEVs) are nanosized membrane-bound nanoparticles naturally secreted by Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. These vesicles mediate intercellular communication through delivery of diverse bioactive cargo, including proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, metabolites, and signaling molecules. Initially recognized as virulence determinants in pathogenic bacteria, BEVs are increasingly recognized as multifunctional platforms with potential applications in sustainable agriculture. This review examines BEV biogenesis, cargo composition, plant uptake, and emerging roles in plant growth promotion, stress adaptation, and disease resistance. Emphasis is placed on BEV-mediated modulation of plant immunity through pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), pattern-triggered immunity (PTI), and induced systemic resistance (ISR). Potential roles of vesicle-associated phytohormones, ACC deaminase, siderophores, extracellular enzymes, and regulatory RNAs in nutrient acquisition, phytohormone homeostasis, and stress responses are critically evaluated. Emerging evidence linking BEVs to drought, salinity, heat, heavy metal, and nutrient-deficiency responses is examined, with emphasis on antioxidant defense, osmotic adjustment, ion homeostasis, and stress-responsive signaling. The review also discusses engineered BEVs as potential biostimulants, nano-biofertilizers, biocontrol agents, and precision delivery systems, including CRISPR-based engineering, synthetic vesicles, AI-guided cargo optimization, and smart nanoformulations. Major challenges include scalable production, standardization, biosafety, regulation, and field validation. However, critical knowledge gaps remain regarding BEV perception, cellular uptake, cargo delivery, and the causal basis of plant responses, together with uncertainties surrounding biosafety, reproducibility, and performance under field conditions. Collectively, BEVs represent promising biological nanocarriers for climate-resilient and sustainable agriculture, but further mechanistic, methodological, and field-based research is required to establish their reliability and practical agricultural potential.

title: Bacterial extracellular vesicles as emerging biostimulants in plant microbe signaling and stress tolerance.

abstract: Due to the increasing demand for clinical gene therapy and the limitations of current treatment methods, there is an urgent need to develop gene-editing tools that are safer, more precise, and more clinically implementable. Deaminase-based base editors have emerged as gene-editing platforms with significant therapeutic potential because they can achieve precise single-base substitutions without inducing DNA double-strand breaks. However, the challenges of applying base editing in clinical practice extend beyond whether the intended edit can be achieved. The critical question is whether the editing system can reliably provide predictable, controllable, and verifiable outcomes across complex sequence contexts, diverse cell environments, and actual delivery conditions. This review focuses on the engineering optimization and clinical translation of base editors. We first systematically analyze the major factors affecting the clinical translation of base editors across four dimensions: editing efficiency, editing precision, safety, and delivery, together with the corresponding optimization strategies. We then summarize the applications of artificial intelligence and computational approaches in base editor design, screening, and risk assessment. We further discuss the ex vivo and in vivo pathways for clinical translation, including their respective requirements for product quality and safety evaluation. Finally, based on representative clinical programs, we discuss how editing performance, safety, and delivery factors influence development decisions for candidate base-editing systems across different therapeutic contexts, and propose minimum reporting recommendations to improve the consistency of key data and cross-study comparability.

abstract: Encapsulation efficiency (EE) estimates the encapsulated fraction of measured RNA in an mRNA lipid nanoparticle (LNP) preparation, whereas particle occupancy measures the fraction of particles containing detectable RNA. Neither metric describes the full distribution of RNA among particles. Particle-resolved studies show that high bulk EE can coexist with RNA-negative particles and broad copy-number distributions, but reported empty-particle fractions vary with composition, preparation, and analytical method. This Minireview examines fluorescence spectroscopy, particle-resolved microscopy and RNA counting, mass spectrometry, and population-separation approaches, distinguishing direct RNA-sensitive measurements from inferred loading. It considers manufacturing determinants and evidence linking payload distributions to product performance. Process changes can alter loading without parallel changes in mean particle size. mRNA-expression, multi-cargo gene-editing, and adjacent siRNA-knockdown studies suggest possible functional consequences, although the independent effect of binary occupancy on potency remains unresolved. Historical lipid-mediated delivery experiments caution against assuming that eliminating RNA-negative particles always improves activity. Occupancy is therefore best considered a context-dependent extended-characterization metric for development and comparability. Product-specific evidence is needed to determine whether occupancy is a critical quality attribute. Its use in routine testing would also require a fit-for-purpose validated analytical procedure and an appropriate control strategy.

abstract: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is the most devastating gastrointestinal emergency in preterm infants, frequently causing mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment1,2. Although the gut microbiota has been implicated in NEC pathogenesis3-5, the microbial factors driving NEC and the following brain pathology remain unclear. Here we identify Clostridium perfringens pathobionts containing Delta toxin in the gut microbiome of individuals with severe and fatal NEC. Clinically, infected infants show worse outcomes, including aberrant systemic inflammation, severe neurological damage and coagulopathy. We establish a mouse model in which Delta-toxin-positive C. perfringens infection, or Delta toxin exposure alone, recapitulates clinical features of NEC, including intestinal necrosis and acute cerebral injury. Mechanistically, Delta toxin preferentially targets macrophages, potently activating inflammasome signalling and pyroptosis, triggering a rapid inflammatory cascade that compromises blood-brain barrier integrity and drives neuroinflammation. Through a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify the tetraspanin CD9 as the host receptor for Delta toxin. Using systemic, myeloid-specific and intestinal-epithelial-specific Cd9-knockout mice, we show that systemic and myeloid Cd9 ablation protects mice against toxin-induced lethality, blood-brain barrier dysfunction and multiorgan injury, whereas epithelial Cd9 deletion shows partial protection, implicating macrophage targeting as a primary driver of C. perfringens CD9-dependent pathogenesis. Furthermore, a neutralizing anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody confers protection against disease progression. These findings suggest that a subset of NEC is a specific-toxin-mediated disorder and validate the Delta toxin-CD9 axis as a therapeutic target for this subset.

abstract: Zebrafish is an excellent in vivo model for high-throughput antiangiogenic drug testing, commonly known as the zebrafish angiogenesis assay. Conventional zebrafish angiogenesis assays are performed in wild-type zebrafish to evaluate the vascular changes in intersegmental and subintestinal vessel regions of the zebrafish larvae at 2 and 3 dpf stages, respectively. However, wild-type zebrafish larvae do not adequately mimic the hypoxia microenvironment and ectopic vessel branching characteristics of cancer. To overcome this limitation, we developed a genetically engineered zebrafish model with constitutive activation of the hypoxia signaling pathway by targeting the vhl, a tumor suppressor, by negative regulation of the hypoxia pathway, using CRISPR mutagenesis. This model exhibits robust ectopic blood vessel branching throughout the larval body, thereby recapitulating pathological angiogenesis. The utility of this zebrafish model system for drug screening was validated with the sorafenib treatment, a known antiangiogenic tyrosine kinase inhibitor. Overall, this proangiogenic hypoxia zebrafish model provides a physiologically relevant platform for testing antiangiogenic drugs. Key features • Generate a vhl mutant zebrafish line with constitutive activation of the hypoxia signaling pathway using CRISPR-CAS9 mutagenesis. • The generated model exhibits extensive ectopic neovascular branching and abnormal vascular growth resembling pathological angiogenesis observed in solid tumors. • Mimics the chronic hypoxic microenvironment commonly associated with cancer progression and angiogenesis. • Provides an economical alternative to mammalian tumor models for early-stage antiangiogenic drug testing.

abstract: Safflower is an Asteraceae oilseed crop valued for its high-quality unsaturated fatty acids (≈90% oleic and linoleic acids), natural floral pigments, and diverse bioactive compounds. These attributes underpin its applications in functional foods, nutraceuticals, pharmaceuticals, and various industrial sectors. Safflower inherent tolerance to drought, heat, cold, and salinity positions it as a climate-resilient alternative to more temperature-sensitive oilseeds; however, omics-based research in this crop remains comparatively fragmented. This review consolidates recent advances across major omics domains. Genomics covers chromosome-scale assemblies, GWAS panels, QTL mapping, and diagnostic candidate genes for molecular breeding. Transcriptomics summarizes regulatory networks for flavonoid and oil biosynthesis, stress-responsive transcription factors (NAC, WRKY, bZIP, AP2/ERF), and seed developmental programs. The proteomics section addresses stress-inducible, therapeutic, and storage/lipid metabolic proteins linked to quality and stress adaptation. Metabolomics outlines quinochalcone and flavonoid pathway architecture, color-specific metabolic profiles, and emerging clinical and nutraceutical applications. Phenomics highlights UAV-based high-throughput phenotyping, RGB and multispectral imaging for salt and drought screening, and machine-learning-assisted germplasm authentication. Epigenomics focuses on DNA methylation and miRNA-mediated regulation. Finally, lipidomics and metagenomics consider oil authentication biomarkers, refining optimization, and microbiome-driven nutrient cycling shaping medicinally important compounds. Despite these advances, critical gaps remain in multi-omics integration, CRISPR-based functional validation, genomic selection pipelines, and detailed characterization of root-shoot architecture under combined stresses. Addressing these gaps will advance mechanistic understanding of climate resilience and enable the development of stress-tolerant, high-yielding safflower cultivars with improved oil quality and bioactive profiles, thereby supporting climate-resilient production systems and high-value safflower-based products at scale.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents a critical global health threat, surpassing the pace of discovery and clinical development of new antimicrobial agents. Therefore, innovative therapeutic strategies are urgently needed to enhance antibiotic efficacy, overcome multidrug-resistant infections, and limit resistance development. Smart liposomal nanoplatforms have emerged as promising tools capable of improving antimicrobial therapy through targeted delivery, enhanced bacterial uptake, biofilm penetration, protection against enzymatic degradation, and controlled drug release.
AREAS COVERED: This review examines recent advances in the rational design of evolved liposomes, including stimuli-responsive and programmable systems, for combating resistant bacterial infections. It discusses their ability to improve pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles, overcome biological barriers, and enable precision antimicrobial delivery. Current translational challenges, including large-scale manufacturing, physicochemical characterization, regulatory requirements, and clinically relevant preclinical models, are critically evaluated. Emerging strategies, such as artificial intelligence-driven formulation optimization, continuous microfluidic manufacturing, multifunctional therapeutic platforms incorporating gene editing, and next-generation antibiotic-adjuvant combination strategies, are also explored.
EXPERT OPINION: Liposomal drug-delivery systems may improve the exposure, distribution, and intracellular or local delivery of antimicrobial agents, but improved delivery should not be equated with reversal of bacterial resistance. Successful clinical translation will depend on formulation- and infection-specific evidence, clinically relevant preclinical models, controlled and scalable manufacturing, and appropriate regulatory frameworks, while artificial intelligence, digital-twin, and precision-medicine approaches are best viewed as decision-support tools that complement experimental and clinical validation.

abstract: The worldwide emergence of antimicrobial resistance and the need for non-conventional alternatives to conventional antibiotics have been increased by multidrug-resistant ESKAPE pathogens, which cause the majority of nosocomial infections and are starting to develop resistance to even the most potent drugs. Engineered bacteriophages are promising precision antimicrobials because of their ability to selectively infect and lyse bacterial hosts, multiply at infection sites, and co-evolve with bacterial populations to overcome resistance. Advances in synthetic biology, such as tail fiber modification, depolymerase and endolysin enhancement, genome editing using the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR), and computationally designed phage cocktails, have opened new possibilities for therapeutics that were hindered by the limitations of natural phages. These engineering strategies expand host range, enhance biofilm penetration, and target resistance genes. In spite of promising evidence in preclinical models, the use of engineered phages in routine clinical practice remains difficult. Specific key challenges include unclear regulations, lack of good manufacturing practice (GMP)grade production, variable pharmacokinetics and limited clinical trial data. This review critically examines engineering approaches to improve phage activity against ESKAPE pathogens, identifies the scientific and regulatory barriers limiting clinical use, and outlines the key steps needed for wider adoption.

abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) intracellular domains (ICDs) couple antigen recognition to T-cell activation. Here we worked with AI agents to refactor CAR ICDs, proposing designs and refining them as measurements accumulated over three rounds. This approach yielded KRGR-{zeta}1-40, a 45-amino-acid ICD less than a third the length of the clinical 4-1BB-CD3{zeta} (BB{zeta}) ICD. Compared with BB{zeta}, KRGR-{zeta}1-40 increased CAR surface expression and antigen-driven IFN-{gamma} release, without detectable antigen-independent IFN-{gamma} release. KRGR-{zeta}1-40 extended CAR expression and target-cell killing after transient mRNA delivery, supported the expression of four CARs from a shared mRNA dose, and enhanced B-cell depletion after lentiviral and lipid-nanoparticle delivery. These results show that iterative agent-guided design with experimental feedback can yield compact ICDs that enhance CAR expression and sustain CAR T-cell function.

abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a rapidly progressing neurodegenerative disorder that selectively affects motor neurons. The median survival time after diagnosis is 2 to 5 years. Oxidative stress (OS), driven mainly by reactive oxygen species (ROS), plays a central role in motor neuron (MN) degeneration. In this narrative review, we analyse the pathogenic role of SOD1 variants and their contribution to OS in ALS. SOD1 mutations alter the Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase enzyme, thereby promoting oxidative damage and triggering neuroinflammatory cascades via the MAPK, NF-κB and Nrf2/ARE signalling pathways. We also discuss emerging proteomic and machine-learning biomarkers, as well as the current therapeutic landscape. Riluzole and edaravone are approved treatments, while AMX0035 was approved in 2022 but withdrawn in 2024. Masitinib and EPI-589 remain investigational. In the realm of genetic therapies, the antisense oligonucleotide tofersen received accelerated FDA approval in 2023 for SOD1-ALS, primarily due to its ability to reduce plasma neurofilament light chain levels. However, the clinical benefit remains modest. RNA interference has reached human trials, while CRISPR/Cas9 remains in the preclinical stage. Both approaches have shown promising results in experimental models. Further research into ALS pathogenesis is needed to develop treatments that integrate antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and gene-editing strategies.

abstract: Chronic lung diseases arise from complex interactions between environmental exposures and host genetic factors. However, these interactions are not fully understood, and despite decades of study, effective curative therapies remain unavailable for many patients. Recent breakthroughs in therapeutic gene-editing have become a reality for some inherited blood diseases and are a promising approach for monogenic lung diseases. Early-phase clinical studies are now ongoing for AATD, primarily through liver-directed editing of hepatocytes to restore circulating functional AAT and for COVID-19 using gene-edited immune cell approaches. However, direct in vivo gene-editing of pulmonary epithelial cells remains largely at the preclinical stage. Expanding this therapeutic pipeline requires overcoming the unique biological barriers of the lung and developing human-specific models that faithfully recapitulate human disease mechanisms. Advances in gene-editing technologies, including CRISPR-Cas9 systems, base and prime editors, and emerging compact nucleases, have increased the feasibility of precise genomic correction. However, safe and efficient delivery directly to the lung remains a major unmet challenge due to mucus, surfactant, epithelial tight junctions, and innate immune surveillance. Delivery systems such as engineered AAVs, lentiviral vectors, selective organ targeting lipid nanoparticles and aerosolizable formulations like nebulised or dry powder nanoparticles are beginning to address these obstacles. In parallel, human preclinical models have evolved from traditional cell lines to more sophisticated platforms such as iPSC-derived airway and alveolar cells, organoids, precision-cut lung slices, air-liquid interface cultures, organ-on-a-chip devices, and patient-derived primary cells. These models enable mechanistic interrogation, variant-specific functional assessment, and preclinical evaluation of gene-editing strategies with increased physiological relevance. In this review, we detail current and emerging gene-editing tools, delivery strategies, and human-relevant disease models. We highlight key translational barriers and discuss how advanced human models combined with improved delivery technologies can accelerate the development of safe and effective gene-editing therapeutics for chronic respiratory disease.

abstract: Background/Objectives: CRISPR/Cas-dependent base editing enables the precise correction of genomic sequences by direct modification of DNA bases without creating potentially mutagenic DNA double-strand breaks. Base editing is considered a therapeutic approach for rare monogenic disorders or viral infections. However, many variants of base editors suffer from limited specificity because they induce bystander edits within a broad editing window. However, nucleotide substitution is sufficient to correct a mutation or to achieve a therapeutic effect. Methods: PCR, cloning by restriction digest, and ligation were used to create genetic constructs. The editing efficiency was evaluated using NGS. Virus-like particles were produced in HEK293T cells using transient expression. VLPs were visualized by electron microscopy. Results: Using dual base editors that induce C-to-T and A-to-G substitutions, we show that high editing precision can be achieved by engineering the linker between the MmCas12m domain and the deaminase domain of the editor. By testing different linker sequences, we have created high-precision dual base editors with narrowed editing windows that can edit a single nucleotide at a target position with high accuracy. Conclusions: We found that shortening the linker to an acceptable length provides a single-nucleotide substitution in vitro with minimal bystander activity (less than 0.8%), while the high-precision MmCas12m dual base editor retains up to 90% of the editing efficiency of the original base editor. These high-precision base editors will be useful in cases where high precision is required, and editing of adjacent nucleotides is undesirable.

abstract: Despite the remarkable clinical success of immunotherapy, its efficacy against hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains severely limited, highlighting an urgent need for novel targets and strategies to overcome immune evasion. Here, we aimed to identify key regulators of HCC immunity via unbiased functional screening and develop a targeted therapy to remodel the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). We performed an in vivo CRISPR-knockout screen using a 4500-gene sgRNA library in syngeneic HCC mouse models. Single-cell RNA sequencing of human HCC tissues and in vivo macrophage-depletion assays were utilized to dissect cellular populations and validate underlying mechanisms. We identified ribosomal protein S19 (RPS19) as a central mediator of HCC immune evasion, whose deletion in HCC cells mitigates the immunosuppressive TME. Mechanistically, scRNA-seq pinpointed tumor-associated macrophages as the key effector subset, whereby complement C5a receptor 1 (C5aR1) transduces RPS19 signals to trigger macrophage-dependent immune suppression. We further constructed SP94-peptide-modified disulfide-bond-containing nanoparticles (SNPSS) for targeted CRISPR-Cas9 delivery. SNPSS efficiently homes to HCC cells, releases payloads within the glutathione-rich TME, downregulates RPS19, reverses immune suppression, and robustly suppresses HCC progression in vivo. Collectively, the RPS19-C5aR1-macrophage axis fuels HCC immune escape, and SNPSS-based RPS19 gene-editing offers a promising strategy to remodel the TME and boost HCC immunotherapy efficacy.

title: In Vivo CRISPR Screen Identifies RPS19 as an Immunotherapy Target in Hepatocellular Carcinoma.

abstract: Background: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is still a global health challenge, as there is no effective treatment due to the inadequacy of conventional experimental platforms for comprehending pathogenic mechanisms and developing therapy. Objectives: This review details the recent progress and clinical utility of next-generation iPSC-derived 3D in vitro systems integrated with microfluidics, CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, multi-omics readouts, and AI-based machine learning, which are emerging as transformative platforms for recapitulating key ALS pathological hallmarks. Methods: A literature search was performed using PubMed and Web of Science, including only English-language publications. All the published papers collected covered the period from January 2015 to June 2026. Results: Human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) cerebral organoids, assembloids, and organ-on-a-chip technologies are revolutionizing research into ALS by providing a way to model the complex spatial organization, cellular heterogeneity, and neural network dynamics of the human brain. Moreover, recent bioengineering advancements enable the inclusion of functional neurovascular units, the integration of resident immune cells (microglia), and the use of 3D bioprinting to accelerate the functional maturation of age-related phenotypes. CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing, OMICS, and machine learning improve tools for studying ALS and identifying therapeutic targets. Conclusions: Novel cell culture models may bridge the gap between preclinical animal models and human clinical trials and reduce the duration and costs of translation. Future work is likely to integrate bioprinting with organ-on-chip microfluidics, CRISPR-based genetic editing, and multi-omics readouts to build increasingly faithful, patient-specific ALS models for both basic research and precision therapeutics.
